passages.text: Short and long-term effects on the thyroid proteome after 131I exposure
Abstract

131I is recognised, both for its significance in nuclear medicine, and for its association with a rise in paediatric but not adult thyroid cancer cases following the Chornobyl accident. However, the detailed radiobiological mechanisms underlying 131I effects on the thyroid remain unknown to date. In the present study, 1 kBq or 100 kBq 131I was administered to mice that were euthanised after 48 h, 3 weeks or 6 months. Thyroid glands were surgically removed, and proteins were extracted and analysed by tandem mass spectrometry. On a group-level, the results showed few alterations in protein abundance, mainly linked to RNA metabolism and DNA damage response. However, individual analysis of protein abundance changes in each animal showed distinct findings suggesting inhibited proliferation in a few individuals across various exposure levels and time points. Future studies should involve larger animal groups to better assess the frequency and variability of proteomic radiation responses.
Introduction

The radioactive iodine isotope 131I is primarily accumulated in the thyroid gland but results in exposure of all organs and tissues in the body, however, to a much lower extent. 131I decays (t1/2 = 8.02 days) by emission of beta particles with an average energy of 0.192 MeV and an average range in tissue of less than 1 mm. Consequently, the majority of the energy of electrons released during 131I decay in the thyroid is absorbed within the thyroid. Due to these properties, 131I has gained a prominent role in nuclear medicine. It is widely employed for the treatment of hyperthyroidism and post-thyroidectomy remnant ablation in thyroid cancer.

However, 131I is also a significant nuclide released in nuclear accident scenarios. It is produced during thermal nuclear fission with a relatively high yield, i.e. the 131I inventory of an operating nuclear reactor core is high, and its chemical properties makes it volatile, thus allowing it to disperse widely in the event of a breach in the reactor vessel. This was demonstrated after the Chornobyl accident, where 131I fallout was detected over large areas in the months following the accident. Epidemiological data indicate that the exposure to 131I of the population in the most affected areas caused a rapid rise in paediatric thyroid cancer cases.

The connection between 131I exposure and thyroid cancer is well established through statistical and epidemiological data. Rearrangements of the RET gene or other receptor tyrosine kinase genes are overrepresented carcinogenesis drivers amongst radiation-induced thyroid cancers, as are mutations in the BRAF gene. Nevertheless, the complex radiobiological mechanisms behind cancer induction due to 131I exposure remain unknown to date. These mechanisms result from a complex interplay amongst different biological processes within the living organism, so to un-puzzle this complexity, in vivo studies become essential. Hence, the focus of the present study was to explore biological changes due to in vivo irradiation of the thyroid from 131I.

The absorbed dose to thyroid received by individuals affected by the Chornobyl 131I fallout varied from a few mGy to a few Gy, generally classified as low to medium absorbed dose. The impact of 131I exposure in the range of a few mGy remains a topic of a lively debate, which underscores the significance of investigating the complete spectrum of potential radiobiological effects associated with such low absorbed doses.

Another noteworthy aspect of thyroid cancer induced by exposure to 131I is the latency period. For other radiation exposure modes, it is normally several decades, whereas the latency period observed after the Chornobyl accident 131I exposure is in general considerably shorter. For comparison, the latency period for radiotherapy-induced thyroid cancer has been reported to be between 20 and 40 years, whereas latencies for paediatric thyroid cancers in the Chornobyl fallout area were reported to be lower than 20 years. This interesting aspect provides an additional dimension to the need to investigate effects that extend beyond immediate mutations. In addition, it becomes apparent that the time aspect is important, and thus, the radiobiological effects are studied at several different time points.

The acute biological effects of high-dose radiation:both ionising and non-ionising:are relatively well understood, but predicting delayed effects that manifest decades later remains challenging. In contrast, our understanding of both acute and delayed effects of low-dose radiation is limited. Acute effects at low doses are often subtle, difficult to detect, and hard to replicate, while the chronic effects of long-term low-dose exposure are largely unknown and cannot be reliably inferred from high-dose data. The physiological relevance of low-dose-induced biological changes is also unclear. Similarly, delayed outcomes from high-dose exposures are unpredictable. Amongst modern 'omics' methods of biomarker discovery within the field of internal irradiation, a lot of focus has been put on gene expression analysis. Proteomics:the global identification and quantification of protein abundances in a cell, is a well-established tool for biomarker research in the fields of pharmacology and toxicology. However, it remains relatively under-utilized in radiation research. Proteomics, especially when integrated with other 'omics' approaches, holds promise for identifying molecular targets of radiation, biomarkers of exposure, and for understanding the biological and health impacts of both acute and delayed radiation effects. One of the reasons for this is that while gene expression analysis provides information on what genes are actively being transcribed in a cell, it is not certain that these changes will result in a net change in expression and activity of the functional proteins. However, the existing proteomics data related to radiation exposure is currently too limited to support robust hypothesis generation regarding long-term health outcomes.

The aim of this work was to determine the proteomic response within thyroids from mice exposed to 131I encompassing different low absorbed dose levels and time points. The abundance of different proteins in specific tissues, i.e. the tissue's proteome, is one indicator of the state of the constituent cells. Certain changes in the proteome may be indicative of the tissue's reactions to different stimuli, e.g. to radiation.
Material and methods
Animal experiments

To assess the radiobiological response to 131I exposure, animal experiments were performed, and in this paper, the proteomic results of these experiments are presented. The study was approved by the Gothenburg Committee for Animal Ethics, Sweden (no. 146-2015).

Forty-five male mice (C57BL/6N, Charles River Laboratories, Germany, age 6-7 weeks) were randomly divided into nine groups of equal size. Three groups each were intravenously injected with, nominally, 100 kBq or 1 kBq 131I (GE Healthcare, Danderyd, Sweden), in 0.1 ml saline, or with 0.1 ml saline as controls. The activity was estimated from the activity concentration of the injected solution and the difference in weight of the syringe before and after injection. The 131I activity in solutions and syringes was assessed by measurement using a gamma counter (Wallac Wizard 3, Wallac Oy, Turku, Finland), which was cross-calibrated to an ionisation chamber (CRC-15 dose calibrator, Capintec, IA, USA) used for activity measurement of the stock solution.

Animals included in each group was housed in a separate cage and all mice were provided with water and standard laboratory rodent chow ad libitum. One group per exposure level was euthanised 48 h, 3 weeks, or 6 months post-injection (Fig. 1). The mice were killed by cardiac puncture under anaesthesia by sodium pentobarbital (60 mg/ml, APL, Sweden). The mean absorbed dose to the thyroid was estimated for each animal based on the administered amount of activity and time of euthanasia. The absorbed dose calculations were based on the Medical Internal Radiation Dose (MIRD) formalism and the data and methods presented by Andersson et al..
Design of the animal experiments. Created with BioRender.com.

Following euthanasia, the thyroid was excised and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. Proteins were extracted using the AllPrep DNA/RNA/Protein kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) following the manual of the provider. RNA and DNA were saved for later studies. The protein concentrations in the solutions submitted for analysis were measured using a Qubit 3.0 fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific), following the manual of the provider.
Proteomic analysis

The extracted proteins were submitted to the Proteomics Core Facility at the University of Gothenburg, where tandem mass tag mass spectrometry (TMT-MS) was used for quantifying relative protein abundances in each individual thyroid.
Sample preparation and digestion

Protein concentration was determined using Pierce 660 Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fischer Scientific) and 30 mug from each sample and three reference samples (mixture of proteins from all groups) were processed by modified filter-aided sample preparation method. In short, samples were transferred to Microcon-Biomax membrane 30 kDa Centrifugal Filter Units (Merck), reduced in 100 mM dithiothreitol at 56 C for 30 min, washed several times with 8 M urea and once with digestion buffer [DB, 50 mM HEPES, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate (SDC)] prior to alkylation with 375 mM iodoacetamide in DB for 30 min in room temperature. Samples were digested with trypsin (Pierce MS grade Trypsin, Thermo Fisher Scientific, ratio 1:50) at 37 C overnight and an additional portion of trypsin was added and incubated for another 3 h. Peptides were collected by centrifugation and labelled using TMTpro 16-plex isobaric mass tagging reagents (Thermo Fisher Scientific) into three sets, according to the manufacturer's instructions. The labelled samples and references were combined into one pooled sample per set, acetonitrile evaporated using vacuum centrifugation, and SDC was removed by acidification with 10% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) and subsequent centrifugation. The TMT-sets were purified using HiPPR detergent removal kit (Thermo Scientific) and Pierce peptide desalting spin columns (Thermo Scientific), according to the manufacturer's instructions prior to basic reversed-phase chromatography fractionation. Peptide separation was performed using a Dionex Ultimate 3000 UPLC system (Thermo Fischer Scientific) and a reversed-phase XBridge BEH C18 column (3.5 mum, 3.0 x 150 mm, Waters Corporation) with a gradient from 3% to 90% acetonitrile in 10 mM ammonium formate at pH 10.00 over 70 min at a flow of 400 muL/min. The 70 fractions were concatenated into 22 fractions, dried and reconstituted in 3% acetonitrile, 0.1% TFA.
NanoLC-MS/MS analysis and database search

Each fraction was analysed on Orbitrap Eclipse  Tribrid  mass spectrometer equipped with the FAIMS Pro ion mobility system interfaced with nLC 1200 liquid chromatography system (all Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were trapped on an Acclaim Pepmap 100 C18 trap column (100 mum x 2 cm, particle size 5 mum, Thermo Fischer Scientific) and separated on an in-house constructed analytical column (350 x 0.075 mm I.D.) packed with 3 mum Reprosil-Pur C18-AQ particles (Dr. Maisch, Germany) using a gradient from 4% to 80% acetonitrile in 0.2% formic acid over 90 min at a flow of 300 nL/min. FAIMS Pro was alternating between the compensation voltages (CV) of -50 and - 70, and essentially the same data-dependent settings were used at both CVs. Precursor ion mass spectra were acquired at 120000 resolution, scan range 375-1375 and maximum injection time 50 ms. MS2 analysis was performed in a data-dependent mode, where the most intense doubly or multiply charged precursors were isolated in the quadrupole with a 0.7 m/z isolation window and dynamic exclusion within 10 ppm for 60 s. The isolated precursors were fragmented by collision-induced dissociation at 35% collision energy with the maximum injection time of 35 ms for 3 s ('top speed' setting) and detected in the ion trap, followed by multinotch (simultaneous) isolation of the top 10 MS2 fragment ions within the m/z range 400-1400, fragmentation (MS3) by higher-energy collision dissociation (HCD) at 55% collision energy and detection in the Orbitrap at 50000 resolution m/z range 100-500 and maximum injection time 105 ms.

The data files for the set were merged for identification and relative quantification using Proteome Discoverer version 2.4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Protein identification and relative quantification was performed in accordance with standard proteomic procedure. The search was against Swissprot mouse database (September 2022) using Sequest as a search engine with precursor mass tolerance of 5 ppm and fragment mass tolerance of 0.6 Da. Tryptic peptides were accepted with one missed cleavage, variable modifications of methionine oxidation and fixed cysteine alkylation, TMT pro-label modifications of N-terminal and lysine were selected. Percolator was used for peptide-spectrum match (PSM) validation with the strict false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of 1%. TMT reporter ions were identified with 3 mmu mass tolerance in the MS3 HCD spectra and the TMT reporter intensity values for each sample were normalised on the total peptide amount. Only the quantitative results for the unique peptide sequences with the minimum spectral pair similarity (SPS) match of 65% and the average S/N above 10 were taken into account for the protein quantification. The quantified proteins were filtered at 5% FDR and grouped by sharing the same sequences to minimise redundancy. All information on protein full names and functions was retrieved from the UniProt database.
Statistical treatment of proteomic data

Raw counts from the TMT-MS analysis were normalised to that of the pooled reference samples to enable comparisons between individuals, yielding relative abundances for each protein in each individual. All analyses based on these relative abundances were carried out using the R statistical computing environment version 4.3.1 (https://www.R-project.org/). The heatmap (Fig. 2) was generated using the package pheatmap.

Heat map showing the statistically significant log2FC values with an absolute value larger than 0.585 for the abundance of proteins for each individual animal, grouped according to experimental group. For exposed individuals, log2FC values are relative to the group average of the corresponding control group. For the control individuals, log2FC are relative to the other four individuals in the same group. The colours indicate the statistically significant log2FC values and grey colour indicates that the log2FC was not statistically significant in the respective individual, or that the log2FC had an absolute value smaller than 0.585. Data are shown only for the 4712 proteins that were found to have an altered abundance in at least one individual, i.e. 474 of the 5186 proteins were excluded because they were not found to have an altered abundance in any of the individuals. The text at the bottom of the heat map states individual identity number for each animal, together with the number proteins with statistically significant altered abundance for each animal. The injected activity and time after injection for each group is shown by colour codes above the heat map.
Group-wise effects

Initially, relative protein abundances were compared at the group level, where results from each group of animals that had received 1 kBq or 100 kBq of 131I, respectively, were compared to corresponding data for its corresponding control group, i.e. the group that had received an injection of saline solution and euthanised at the same time point after injection.

Group means and standard deviations were calculated from log2 of the relative abundance data for each protein, and P-values were computed with Welsh's t-test for statistically significant differences in relative abundance for each protein. These P-values were then corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg method, to reduce the FDR. Differences in relative abundance were regarded as statistically significant if the adjusted P-value (i.e. the q-value) was below 0.05. Fold changes (FCs) were calculated as the difference in the log2 of the group means. An FC was regarded as relevant if the absolute value of the FC exceeded 1.5, i.e. if the change in relative protein abundance exceeded 50%. The conditions lFCl > 1.5 (llog2FCl < 0.585) and q < 0.05 were applied, resulting in a list of proteins with statistically significant and relevant differences in protein abundances for each exposed group, relative to its control group. In the following, abundances are referred to as altered (or higher/lower) if the difference in relative abundance is both statistically significant and relevant according to these criteria.
Individual effects

Individual effects within each exposed animal relative to its respective control group were also studied. In order to make such a comparison, relative protein abundances from every exposed individual were compared with the corresponding mean values for the corresponding control group using a one-sample t-test. As in previous analyses, q-values were calculated by adjusting the P-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. The proteins were considered to have an altered relative abundance under the same criteria as previously stated, i.e. lFCl > 1.5 and q < 0.05. When studying individual effects on relative protein abundances, it is important to also assess the individual variability in the proteome to, if possible, distinguish natural variations from radiation-induced variations. To do this, the relative protein abundances for each individual within each of the three control groups were analysed in comparison to the other four individuals in the same control group. Again, a one-sample t-test was used, P-values were Benjamini-Hochberg corrected, and the same thresholds for FC and q were used as before.
Pathway analysis

Pathway analyses were performed using gene set enrichment analysis, as implemented in the R package ReactomePA. The FCs for the set of proteins with altered relative abundance (lFCl > 1.5 and q < 0.05) were submitted for each group as well as for each individual. The pathway analysis as performed with the package ReactomePA takes the magnitude of FC into account, and thus makes it possible to identify pathways as regulated either through a large FC in one or a few key proteins, or through small but consistent FC in a number of proteins associated with the same pathway. The statistical significance of the FC is, in this analysis, taken into account by only basing the analysis on the FC which were significant with a q < 0.05.

Statistical analyses were exclusively performed on these 5186 proteins that were detected in all three sets, for both group wise effects and individual effects.
Group-wise effects

For the mice exposed to 1 kBq 131I and euthanised after 48 h, the abundance of Selenoprotein M (SELM) was found to be increased. This protein may function as a thiol-disulphide oxidoreductase that participates in disulphide bond formation. For the mice exposed to 100 kBq 131I and euthanised after 48 h, the abundance of TP53-binding protein 1 (TP53BP1) was reduced. Amongst the mice euthanised after 3 weeks, no protein exhibited significant alterations in abundance. Also for the mice exposed to 1 kBq and euthanised after 6 months, no alterations were found, but amongst the mice exposed to 100 kBq 131I and euthanised after 6 months, four proteins had altered abundances (Table 2).
Pathway analysis

For the four proteins found to have an altered abundance in the group exposed to 100 kBq of 131I and euthanised after 6 months, no pathways were found to be regulated with a threshold FDR > 0.05. However, four pathways were found regulated with FDR values ranging from 0.12 to 0.24, and these pathways were all associated with RNA metabolism.
Individual effects

A heat map of the log2FC values for all proteins that were altered at a statistically significant level in some of the individuals is shown in Fig. 2. When assessing individual effects, the number of proteins with altered abundances was relatively higher for most individuals in comparison with the group-wise effects. At the 48-h time point, all individuals displayed some proteins with altered abundances, whereas at the later time points, only some of the individuals did. At the 6-month time point, the group that received 100 kBq of 131I showed some proteomic response in all individuals, while the 1 kBq group showed a much weaker response.

One of the individuals in the control group for the 6-month time point (I5) showed a proteome that deviates distinctly from the other four individuals in the same control group. The analysis for the 1 kBq and 100 kBq groups at this time point was repeated, excluding this deviating individual, but the results of the analysis were similar in terms of number of proteins and pathways altered at a statistically significant level. Hence, the results of the analysis include all five individuals in the control group.

The clustering of the rows in Fig. 2 did not reveal any distinct pattern. Clustering of the columns did not group individuals together according to either dose or time point, so the shown column order is based on experimental groups. Inspection of the heatmap, and a statistical analysis of the number of regulated proteins for each individual shows that there was no statistically significant difference in the number of proteins with altered abundance between the two dose levels at 48 h (P = 0.20) or 3 weeks (P = 0.95), whereas at 6 months, there are significantly (P = 0.0043) more proteins with altered abundance for the individuals in the 100 kB group compared with those in the 1 kBq group. The number of proteins with altered abundance is higher in the 48-h time point than at the later time points. The difference is statistically significant comparing the 48-h groups with the 6-month groups (P = 0.027). For the 3-week time point, the difference is not statistically significant (P = 0.12), due to the large variance at the 3-week time point caused by the outliers D1 and E4. There is also no statistically significant difference in the number of proteins with altered abundance between the 3-week and 6-month time points.
Pathway analysis

No pathways were found to be regulated in any of the exposed individuals euthanised after 6 months.

As can be seen in Table 3, pathways belonging only to 16 of the 27 top-level pathways are affected at a statistically significant level in any of the individuals, and amongst these, there is a clear over-representation for only a few top-level pathways; 'Metabolism of proteins', 'Metabolism of RNA', 'Metabolism', 'Cell cycle', and 'Signal transduction'. Pathways sorted under 'DNA repair' were only found to be regulated in two individuals (B1 and E4), belonging to the groups injected with 1 kBq and sacrificed after 48 h (B1) and 3 weeks (E4).

In four of the individuals exposed to 1 kBq (B1, B3, B5 and E4), pathways sorted under 'Metabolism of proteins' and 'Metabolism of RNA' were clearly overrepresented. The pathways grouped under 'Metabolism of RNA' were more specifically related to 'nonsense-mediated decay' and the pathways grouped under 'Protein metabolism' were mainly related to 'cap-dependent translation initiation'. A similar response, with regulation of the same pathways, was observed in one control individual at the 48-h time point (C6).

Regulation of pathways sorted under 'Cell cycle' were found to be regulated in individuals at both exposure levels, and mostly at the 48-h time point. These pathways were related to the M phase in all six individuals (A1, A4, B1, B3, B5 and E4), and exclusively with a negative enrichment score, i.e. down-regulated. Pathways grouped under 'Cell cycle' were not found in any of the control individuals. In the individuals where several pathways were regulated, the response was quite coherent. The regulated pathways related to cell cycle were: 'Cell cycle' (found to be regulated in four individuals), 'Cell cycle', 'mitotic', 'M phase', 'Cell cycle checkpoints', 'Mitotic prometaphase', 'Resolution of sister chromatid cohesion', 'Mitotic metaphase and anaphase', 'Mitotic Anaphase' and 'Separation of sister chromatids'.

The pathways grouped under 'Signal transduction' were mainly related to 'signalling by Rho GTPases' in four of the individuals (A1, A4, B1, D1 and I5), the pathways grouped under 'Metabolism' were mainly related to the 'citric acid cycle' (A3, B1, D1, B4 and F3) and the pathways grouped under 'Muscle contraction' were mainly related to 'striated muscle contraction' and 'ion homeostasis' (B1, B4 A1, A4, D1, I5). Note that these pathways are regulated in both exposed and unexposed individuals.
Method robustness

When comparing each control individual to the other four individuals in the same control groups, some individual variations in the control animals' proteomes (manifested as differences in protein abundances from the other individuals in the same group) were identified in seven of the 15 control individuals. In only three cases, the pathway analysis resulted in regulated pathways. These results are also shown in Table 3. In two of the three cases, the pathways were related to the top-level pathways 'Metabolism' (F3 and I5), 'Muscle contraction' (I5), and 'Immune system' (F3). For one individual (C6) in the youngest (48 h) control group, the set of regulated pathways were similar to those identified in irradiated individuals and indicated deviations in pathways related to 'nonsense mediated decay' and 'cap-dependent translation initiation'.
Discussion

131I, a prominent fission product of nuclear reactors, is released into the atmosphere during severe nuclear disasters. Exposure to 131I has been linked with induction of thyroid cancer, but the radiobiological mechanisms underlying this response are poorly understood. This study aimed to assess the proteomic response in thyroids from mice exposed to different amounts of 131I at different times after injection. The results show a variable response in individual animals, resulting in minor changes in group averaged protein abundance. However, examining individual changes in protein abundance within each animal revealed distinct findings indicative of DNA damage response in select individuals across different exposure levels and time points.
Group-wise effects

The fact that the abundance of the tumour suppressor protein TP53BP1 was found to be lowered in the 100 kBq group at the 48-h time point is according to expectation. At 48 h after injection, the dose rate is relatively high and radiobiological damage and repair processes are ongoing. An altered abundance indicates that double-strand break repair processes are activated, and specifically, a lowered abundance of TP53BP1 favours homologous repair over nonhomologous end joining. Previous studies found increased numbers of TP53BP1 nuclear foci in irradiated mouse thyroid follicular cells 1 month after irradiation, which might be an indication of over-expression of this protein in response to previous DNA damage.

The exact function of SELM, which was found in an increased abundance in the 1 kBq group at the 48-h time point, is not well understood to date. However, one of its suggested functions is chemically reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS). Since the production of ROS is a well-known consequence of ionising radiation exposure, the increased abundance of SELM suggests a thyroid response to oxidative stress and indirect radiation damage. The lack of SELM increase in the 100 kB group at 48 h should be noted and might indicate a dose threshold for this pathway.

Four proteins were found to have an altered abundance for the 100 kBq group at the 6-month time point. These proteins were not related to any shared signalling pathway. The Matrix Gla protein is involved in transcription regulation and the Probable ATP-dependent RNA helicase DDX46 plays an essential role in splicing A complex formation. The UPF0415 protein C7orf25 homologue is suggested to be involved in the proteasome pathway, and Serpin B5 is involved in the p53 signalling pathway. Although these proteins do not seem to share any function, the fact that their abundance was found to be altered in a group-wise comparison indicates that the long-term response is stronger than the short- and medium-term response in terms of altered protein abundances, with a larger (albeit small) number of proteins with altered abundances at the 6-month time point, compared with no proteins with altered abundances at the 3-week time point.

Previous studies of the rodent thyroid proteome after radiation exposure from 131I have also identified proteins that, in group-wise comparisons, have altered abundances. Rudqvist et al. used female Balb/c nude mice, injected with 490 kBq 131I and euthanised 24 h after injection. Larsson et al. used male Sprague Dawley rats injected with 0.5-500 kBq 131I and euthanised 9 months after injection. None of the proteins identified as having altered abundance in their studies were the same as those identified in the group-wise comparisons in this study, most probably due to differences in absorbed dose to thyroid and studied time-points after 131I injection.
Individual effects

Given the stochastic nature of the effects of ionising radiation in the long term and at low absorbed doses, individual effects for each exposed animal relative to its respective control group were analysed. For some individuals a large number of proteins had altered abundances, whereas for six individuals within the same groups (same exposure and time point), the radiation exposure did not result in any significant alterations of protein abundances. This supports the existing evidence that the response to ionising radiation has a significant stochastic element, and that radiosensitivity is highly individual in mice as well as in humans. Furthermore, only in 11 of the 24 individuals that exhibited any significant protein abundance alterations, the proteomic response was coherent enough to result in a significant regulation of a certain pathway. No pathways were found to be regulated in any of the exposed individuals euthanised after 6 months.

The larger number of proteins with altered abundance at the 48-h time point, compared with the other time points, might partly be due to the younger age of the mice at the time of euthanasia. The younger age implies an ongoing development, which could introduce a large variability, as has been indicated in previous studies. The number of proteins in the control mice whose abundance deviates from that in the other control individuals, however, is rather small, indicating that most of the alterations in protein abundances observed in the exposed individuals are indeed due to the exposure and not to natural variability at the young age. It should also be noted that the 48-h groups received a smaller dose than the groups at the later time points, since they were euthanised while exposure was still ongoing. At the later time points, the number of proteins with altered abundance is in general smaller, but several groups comprise some strong outlier. This might be interpreted as a subset of the several proteomic differences (radiation-induced or not) found at a young age, leading to larger deviations if allowed to develop over a longer time span.

Amongst the radiation-exposed individuals the response in terms of regulated pathways was to some extent coherent. As previously stated, only a few top-level pathways were found to be regulated, most importantly 'Metabolism of proteins', 'Metabolism of RNA', 'Metabolism', 'Cell cycle' and 'Signal transduction'. In four of the individuals exposed to 1 kBq (B1, B3, B5 and E4) and one of the control individuals (C6), the pathways grouped under 'Metabolism of RNA' were mostly related to 'Nonsense-mediated decay', a surveillance pathway that reduces errors in gene expression by eliminating aberrant mRNAs that may arise as a result of mutations. For the same individuals, the pathways grouped under 'Metabolism of proteins' were mostly related to 'Cap-dependent translation initiation', the dysregulation of which has been found to be related to cancer. The indication that unrepaired mutations have indeed occurred at the lowest dose level could be interpreted as supporting the hypothesis that there is a dose threshold for activation of DNA repair processes.

The many instances of down-regulated pathways connected with the mitotic phase of the cell cycle indicates that the exposure has caused an inhibition of cell proliferation, although this response is only found in 5 out of 10 exposed individuals at the 48-h time point. A similar proteomic response in terms of regulated pathways is also found in one individual 3 weeks after exposure, which indicates that the effect might be persistent over time in some cases. Cell cycle arrest has been observed in vitro at a dose of 100 mGy x-rays although the detailed mechanisms are still unknown. From this study, we cannot conclude if this response is equally common in the groups exposed to 1 kBq and 100 kBq. A repeated experiment with larger group sizes could indicate if the frequency of this response is dose dependent.

It could be argued that the detected alterations of protein abundances might be a result of individual variations not related to the radiation exposure. The assessment of individual variations of protein abundances within the unexposed control groups revealed variations on a pathway level, corresponding to variations, which might be expected to occur naturally on an individual level (such as an immune response to an incurred infection). However, for the control individual C6, pathways were found to be regulated (relative to the other four individuals in the same control group) related to 'nonsense-mediated decay' and 'cap-dependent translation initiation' and thus, as discussed above, indicative of mutations and cancer. This finding may indicate the occurrence of a spontaneous mutation; thyroid follicular adenomas have been found to occur spontaneously in C57BL mice, but it also points to the difficulty of determining if a response in a single individual is related to radiation exposure or not. The many deviations in the proteome found in the 6 months old control individual (I5) may also be related to a spontaneously occurring thyroid disorder, although the pathway analysis did not point towards mutations or cancer induction.

Two of the proteins found by Rudqvist et al. to have an increased abundance on a group level at 24 h (RL24 and RL5) were also found to have increased abundances in the two individuals in our study that were exposed to 1 kBq of 131I and euthanised after 48 h and responded with regulations of pathways associated with 'Metabolism of proteins' and 'Metabolism of RNA'. RL24 and RL5 are both large ribosomal subunit proteins and are thus associated with protein synthesis. The individual response of each animal in the present study was also compared with the list of 133 proteins found by Larsson et al. to have increased abundances based on group-wise analysis in thyroids from rats 9 months after 131I injection. On average, 1.5% of the proteins that were found to have altered abundances in our study overlapped with the list of proteins identified as regulated by Larsson et al., which is close to the overlap of the list with the total number of probed proteins (1.8%). The overlap ranged between 0 and 5.3% and was not larger for the 6-month group (which is closer in age to the rats in the experiment by Larsson et al. than for the two earlier time points). There thus does not seem to be any correlation between our results and those of Larsson et al. and thus, finding the same proteins to be regulated in the two studies is likely to be coincidental.

The commonly made assumption when comparing groups that have been exposed to different stimuli is that all individuals in a group will react similarly to the same stimuli, i.e. the same cellular processes will be regulated, resulting in similar changes in the proteome. Thus, the commonly practiced way of analysing proteomic data from such experiments is to make group wise comparisons. The immediate cellular response to radiation-induced DNA damage can be described in terms of, e.g. activated processes for DNA damage repair. However, the action of ionising radiation on the DNA is an inherently stochastic process. The cell's ability to repair radiation-induced DNA damage depends, amongst other things, on the DNA lesion type, which is stochastic. Furthermore, the cellular consequences of a non- or misrepaired DNA lesion depend on, amongst other factors, which part of the genome that was damaged, which is also fundamentally stochastic(57). It has been hypothesised that this becomes particularly pronounced at very low doses, below which the normal DNA repair processes are not activated. Furthermore, the exposure resulting from in situ decay of 131I (as opposed to external beam radiation) results in low dose rates, since the dose is delivered during the course of several days. In this context, DNA damage and repair processes are ongoing simultaneously, further adding to the complexity of the induced processes and feedback mechanisms. Thus, the proteomic response to low dose, low dose rate exposure to ionising radiation can be expected to have an important stochastic component and may not be similar in all exposed individuals. For this reason, we here investigated two approaches to TMT-MS data analysis of the mouse thyroid tissue proteome; firstly, the commonly practiced way of assessing group-wise effects, and secondly assessing individual effects. Although the group size in this explorative study is small due to ethical considerations, previous studies have observed statistically significant differences in protein expression using similar methods and similar number of animals per group in mice and rats treated with radioiodine, as well as mice treated with 0.5 Gy whole body external beam irradiation. From these previous experiences, we were surprised about the high variability seen within the treatment groups in this study. However, the results of the individual analysis indicate that this may indeed be a useful approach that could be applied in future studies with larger group sizes. Such studies could also include a wider and more frequent ranges of injected activities to further characterise responses depending on absorbed dose.
Variability

The calculated absorbed dose delivered to each animal's thyroid varied to a small extent within the groups (relative standard deviations of 3%-10%) but given the scarcity of dose-dependent observations when comparing groups with a difference in dose of two orders of magnitude, the within-group dose variations is not expected to contribute significantly to the variability of the results.

The number of proteins identified as having significantly altered abundances was, for the group-wise analysis, quite small. In general, the calculated FCs were often large, but not statistically significant. This indicates a large variability. The technical variability in the TMT-MS method for quantification of relative protein abundances is relatively small:~4% relative standard deviation. Since an entire thyroid lobe from each animal was used for the extractions, sampling variability can be expected to contribute only to a small extent, except for the possibility that small amounts of adjacent tissue might have been included in the thyroid samples. Hence, the variability can be assumed to either originate from the extraction process or to be of biological origin, i.e. due to differences in thyroid state and function between the animals. Note in particular that the suggested regulation of pathways related to 'Muscle contraction' is likely to be an artefact of contamination with muscle tissue, since the thyroid in itself is void of muscle tissue. Despite the limited number of statistically significant individual protein changes, pathway analysis remains valuable because it can detect coordinated, biologically meaningful shifts across groups of related proteins. Small but consistent changes in multiple pathway components may reflect underlying biological processes that are not evident at the single-protein level. This approach helps overcome limitations of statistical power, reduces the impact of multiple testing corrections, and provides system-level insights into the affected biological mechanisms.

Due to the small size of the thyroid and the intent to perform multi-omics studies based on the available samples, the protein extractions were carried out using the Qiagen AllPrep kit. Increasing the group sizes would be questionable from an ethical point of view. The parallel extraction of DNA, RNA, and proteins through the use of so-called multi-omics kits, in this case the Qiagen AllPrep kit, enables multi-omics studies based on a single tissue sample but is not optimal for high-yield protein extractions. Nevertheless, the total protein mass needed for the TMT-MS analysis (30 mug) was extracted from each analysed thyroid lobe. It has also been shown that the extraction efficiency may vary between proteins, with a preference for acidic proteins in the Qiagen AllPrep kit. However, since the extraction method, and hence differences in extraction efficiencies, is the same for the control groups as for the exposed groups, the calculated differences in the relative abundances should not be affected by this. Furthermore, the normalization carried out through the use of pooled reference samples eliminates the effects of potential differences in overall extraction efficiencies between samples. Nevertheless, the non-optimal protein extraction process may contribute to the large observed protein abundance variability.

Another limitation of the used method is that a large number of probed proteins (2179 proteins, i.e. 30% of the 7365 probed proteins) were excluded from the analysis because they were not found in all three TMT sets, which would bias any comparisons involving these proteins. These proteins were excluded as their absence elsewhere likely reflects technical variability, such as stochastic sampling or ion suppression, rather than true biological differences. In TMT-based experiments, quantitative reliability requires consistent detection and reporter ion measurement across samples; proteins identified sporadically lack the robustness needed for valid comparison. Focusing on commonly detected proteins ensures reliable quantification, valid statistical testing, and improves the robustness, interpretability, and reproducibility of the results.

Furthermore, the study was performed on mice and not humans of ethical reasons. Murine models (mice and rats) are then commonly used in biomedical research since it is well known that they resemble humans physiologically in many ways. Ca 99% of the genes in mice resemble those in humans, which facilitates the translation of effects found in mice to that in humans. Murine models are also easily available and cost-effective as surrogates for humans. However, results from mice should as far as possible be validated in humans in order to utilise this information in medical applications or after accidental exposure.
Conclusions

The study indicates that, at a group level, irradiation of the thyroid after intravenous injection of 100 kBq 131I leads to long-term alterations of the abundances of a small number of proteins. These proteins are potentially associated with RNA metabolism, although without statistical significance. In the short term, the exposure triggers a proteomic response associated with DNA damage and increased concentrations of ROS. For other time points and exposure levels, the group-wise analysis did not yield any statistically significant results.

When considering individual effects, many more relative protein abundance alterations and connected pathway regulations were found, although only in a subset of individuals in each group, which ought to be the reason why these alterations were not observed in the group-wise analysis. The most prominent response was inhibition of proliferation, which was found in half of the individuals at an early time point. In general, the cellular response to radiation exposure at the studied dose levels and dose rates appears to be stochastic in the sense that a certain response might occur in only a, seemingly random, subset of individuals. To observe such response, data analysis should be carried out at an individual rather than a group level. With larger group sizes than those used in this study, the frequency of a certain response in different groups can be assessed. Such analyses would add an important information on radiation response at a population level, in addition to the information, which is obtainable through group-wise analysis. The occurrence of a certain response in unexposed individuals must also be studied to correctly estimate the probability that a certain variation in, e.g. the proteome of an individual is unrelated to the exposure.

Studies are ongoing to enhance the current findings by further analysing the effect of 131I exposure on DNA methylation and gene expression. The aim is to validate the findings presented here by establishing correlations between the proteomic response and changes in the transcriptome, genome, or epigenome.

Although the resemblance in physiology and genome is high between mice and humans, radiobiological effects and mechanisms cannot readily be translated to humans, but must be validated in humans as far as possible.

passages.text: Expansion of the Phenotype of Lymphatic Anomalies Caused by Somatic Activating BRAF Variant
Background:

The somatic activating variant in BRAF (p.V600E) was recently described as a novel cause of macrocystic head and neck lymphatic malformations in three individuals. Other recent studies profiling the genetic causes of more complex lymphatic anomalies identified this same pathogenic BRAF variant. Our aim was to expand the phenotypic description of the somatic BRAF p.V600E variant in individuals with vascular anomalies.

annotations.text: macrocystic head and neck lymphatic malformations

passages.text: Procedure:

We searched the database of individuals with vascular anomalies at our institution for those identified as having complex lymphatic anomalies and somatic BRAF p.V600E variants. A comprehensive retrospective review of identified individuals' electronic health records was conducted.
Results:

Six individuals with complex lymphatic anomalies had the BRAF p.V600E variant. All individuals had diffuse lymphatic malformations and abnormal lymphatic conduction. The conduction abnormalities were observed only after surgical interventions in five of the patients, in some cases, manifesting years later. There was immense phenotypic heterogeneity within the cohort.
Conclusions:

Complex lymphatic anomalies are an important new phenotype associated with the pathogenic BRAF p.V600E variant. Even in initially asymptomatic individuals within this patient population, longitudinal follow-up is necessary, and surgical intervention should be pursued with caution. Further investigation is needed to better understand the etiology of the conduction problems associated with this pathogenic variant to inform the multidisciplinary approach to treatment.
Introduction

Complex lymphatic anomalies (CLA), which include generalized lymphatic anomaly (GLA), kaposiform lymphangiomatosis (KLA), Gorham Stout disease (GSD), and central conducting lymphatic anomaly (CCLA), are a highly morbid group of disorders characterized by abnormal development of lymphatic vessels resulting in diffuse lymphatic malformations (LM) and impaired lymphatic flow manifesting as effusions. Specific diagnosis of a CLA is made based on a combination of clinical presentation, imaging features, and histopathology (though often this is not available), but can be complicated by broad phenotypic heterogeneity as well as overlapping clinical features within this group of disorders.

GLA is notable for multifocal LM involving the soft tissues, thoracic and abdominal viscera and cavities, and bone. The bony involvement is often noncontiguous and does not result in destruction of the bone cortex. Affected tissue demonstrates dilated lymphatic channels that stain positive for D2-40 and PROX-1 (markers of lymphatic endothelium). KLA is similar to GLA in its areas of involvement, but commonly also involves coagulopathy with hemorrhagic effusions, and tends to have greater morbidity and higher risk of cardiopulmonary compromise due to its progressive and infiltrative nature. Individuals with KLA frequently have markedly elevated levels of angiopoietin-2, and histopathology demonstrates spindled lymphatic endothelial cells. GSD, or "vanishing bone disease," classically involves the bone in a contiguous pattern and results in progressive osteolysis with destruction of the bone cortex, but may also involve soft tissues and viscera. Evidence of this bony destruction on imaging is critical for the diagnosis, and histopathology demonstrates similar findings to GLA in addition to increased osteoclast activity. CCLA is caused by dysfunction of or improper drainage into the thoracic duct and retrograde reflux of lymphatic fluid with leakage resulting in pleural or pericardial effusions, ascites, protein-losing enteropathy, or generalized edema. Lymphatic imaging is typically necessary to make this diagnosis.

Increased availability of somatic genetic testing has led to the identification of multiple pathogenic variants as causes of these disorders, though an unclear genotype-phenotype correlation remains. Identification of the genotype may help to classify these diagnoses more accurately and offer insight into optimal treatments. Therefore, further understanding of the molecular etiology of these diseases is critical.

The somatic activating variant BRAF c.1799T>A p.Val600Glu (V600E) was recently described as a novel cause of macrocystic head and neck LM in three individuals. This variant had been previously reported to cause other vascular anomalies, but this was the first association of this gene with lymphatic anomalies. Since then, this variant has been attributed to three cases of CCLA in publications by our institution. Here, we expand upon these studies to describe six cases of GLA, KLA, and/or CCLA associated with the BRAF variant, including the three individuals previously reported as well as three new individuals. These results expand the phenotypic description of this BRAF variant beyond isolated LMs to include CLAs.
Methods

We conducted a single-center retrospective chart review at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) with all the data obtained as of February 2025. Inclusion criteria were patients with a confirmed BRAF V600E variant and a diagnosis of CLA. We queried the patient database at our institution for all patients with CLA and included those with a BRAF V600E variant. We have received an IRB exemption for this study. Genetic testing included the University of Pennsylvania Genetic Diagnostic Laboratory Somatic Overgrowth and Vascular Malformation (SOVM) Panel, CHOP's Division of Genomic Diagnostics Solid Tumor Panel, and CHOP's Center for Applied Genomics (CAG) research genetic panel.
Case Descriptions

Patient #1 was diagnosed with an isolated LM of the mesentery and gluteal region on computed tomography (CT) imaging as a neonate (Figure 1A) and underwent resection of a large portion of the mesenteric mass and partial resection of the sigmoid colon at 11 days old, followed by colostomy closure at 4 months. She then had minimal follow-up until 13 years later, when she was incidentally found to have a left-sided chylothorax on scoliosis imaging. Dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance lymphangiography (DCMRL) demonstrated disconnected inguinal and central lymphatic system and dilated thoracic duct draining to collateral lymphatic network, extending through subcutaneous tissue and left paravertebral posterior intercostal lymphatic networks (Figure 1B,C). She underwent glue embolization of left-sided paravertebral and posterior intercostal lymphatic networks, and required bilateral lymphovenous anastomosis of the inguinal skin 1 year later due to weeping lymphatic blebs in the gluteal region. Pathology from a colon resection shows dilated submucosal lymphatic channels (Figure 4A,B) and irregular mesentery lymphatics. A biopsy of the gluteal skin shows mildly dilated and irregularly shaped lymphatics in the deep dermis (Figure 4C). Lymphatics were positive for D2-40 and PROX1. At this point, overall findings were consistent with a diagnosis of CCLA. Genetic testing from the biopsy also demonstrated a somatic BRAF V600E variant at 2.2%-2.6% variant allele frequency (VAF). She was treated with sirolimus for 3 years with no clinical improvement, then transitioned to trametinib for 5 months until dermatologic toxicities, mainly persistent acne, became severe with little improvement in her condition. She was then started on a BRAF inhibitor, vemurafenib, but discontinued after 2 months due to several toxicities, including nausea, weight loss, muscle aches, and hand contractures, coupled with a lack of improvement. Though she continues to have chronic pain and discomfort, her pleural effusion has resolved, and she is able to participate in activities of daily living despite no medical treatment for 2 years.

passages.text: Patient #2, with a history of left inguinal hernia repair as a toddler, was incidentally diagnosed with "lymphangiomatosis" involving the mediastinum, spleen, and mesentery on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure 1D,E) at age 3 as part of a workup for fever without a source. She was largely asymptomatic at the time and subsequently followed for 3 years before being lost to follow-up. At age 15, she presented with bacterial pneumonia complicated by bilateral bloody chylothorax. CT imaging showed a large left pleural effusion, and subsequent MRI confirmed extensive macrocystic and microcystic lymphatic malformations in the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with splenic involvement, perivascular thickening of central vessels, and confluent marrow replacement in the vertebral bodies (Figure 1F). She had normal coagulation studies, but a markedly elevated angiopoietin-2 level of 11,759 pg/mL in blood (reference range: 1434-4141 pg/mL). Research genetic testing of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) isolated from pleural lymphatic fluid revealed a somatic BRAF V600E variant at 0.2%-2.2% VAF. Magnetic resonance lymphangiography (MRL) was performed after the genetic finding revealed abnormal lymphatic drainage into the mediastinum, chest, abdomen, and pelvis (Figure 1G,H). Additionally, biopsy of the right pleura showed irregular, dilated, thin-walled vascular spaces lined by CD31+ , D2-40+ , and PROX1+ endothelial cells, altogether consistent with lymphatics (Figure 4D-F). Features from radiology, clinical presentation, pathology, and genetics led to a diagnosis of KLA with central conduction abnormality. She was initially treated with sirolimus, changed to selumetinib once the BRAF variant was found, and then treated with dual therapy with sirolimus and selumetinib. However, she continued to have recurrent worsening of her chylothoraces requiring frequent thoracentesis and hospitalization. As such, she recently transitioned to dual therapy with dabrafenib and trametinib and underwent lung decortication and selective glue embolization. She has demonstrated substantial clinical improvement since this surgery and the dual therapy with dabrafenib and trametinib.

At 16 months, Patient #3 was incidentally found to have a well-circumscribed mass in the posterior mediastinum and numerous splenic lesions on CT imaging of the chest obtained after recurrent acute respiratory infections (Figure 2A,B). Biopsy of the chest mass demonstrated a combined venous (CD34+, D240-, PROX1 variable) and lymphatic (D240+) components with focal papillary endothelial proliferation. He developed chylothorax after the biopsy for which he required thoracentesis with chest tube placement; the effusion gradually improved with dietary modification and octreotide, but did not fully resolve. At 3 years old, he underwent DCMRL, which showed hepatopulmonary perfusion leaking into the left pleural space and a dilated and tortuous thoracic duct connecting the veins and mediastinal lymphatic malformation (Figure 2D), along with selective glue embolization. Overall findings were consistent with the diagnosis of GLA with central conduction abnormality. Research genetic testing of cfDNA isolated from thoracic duct lymphatic fluid and posterior mediastinal mass biopsy identified a somatic BRAF V600E variant at 0.4% and 1.3% VAF, respectively. He responded well to diuretics and the embolization procedure and did not require targeted pharmacotherapies. The patient has remained healthy without evidence of recurrent chylothorax or lymphatic conduction abnormality for nearly 3 years.

Patient #4 was diagnosed with "lymphangiomatosis" in the mesentery and spleen on MRI (Figure 2E) at age 3, at which time she underwent excision of an abdominal LM and splenectomy. Pathology from the LM showed abnormal thin-walled lymphatic channels filled with proteinaceous fluid and irregular mural smooth muscle that showed patchy D2-40 positivity with diffuse PROX1 and CD31 staining (Figure 4G-I). She remained in good health until age 16, when she presented with protein-losing enteropathy (PLE). Subsequent MRI showed cystic lesions in the chest and retroperitoneum as well as pleural effusions. DCMRL demonstrated cystic abdominal collections with intercostal and duodenal lymphatic perfusion (Figure 2F-H). Overall findings were consistent with a diagnosis of GLA with central conduction abnormality. Genetic testing of the abdominal tissue excised 13 years prior demonstrated a somatic BRAF V600E variant at 8% VAF. She responded well to diuretics and a low-fat, high-protein diet and did not require targeted pharmacotherapies.

Patient #5 had a prenatal ultrasound suspicious for intestinal atresia, but MRI at birth demonstrated diffuse LM in the neck and abdomen, consistent with GLA. She was started on sirolimus at 2 months of age and initially did well on this medication until she developed PLE and anasarca at 16 months of age. DCMRL demonstrated mesenteric LM with bowel wall involvement as well as impaired communication between the mesenteric and central lymphatic systems (Figure 3A-D). At this point, the diagnosis evolved to that of GLA with central conduction abnormality. Genetic testing of cfDNA from pleural lymphatic fluid demonstrated a somatic BRAF V600E variant at 0.2% VAF. She has responded well to treatment with sirolimus and a low-fat diet.

Patient #6 was prenatally diagnosed with hydrops and small bowel obstruction and born prematurely at 29 weeks of gestational age. She underwent exploratory laparotomy with repair of gastric perforation on day of life 5. MRI demonstrated large volume ascites and diffuse LM involving the chest and inguinal areas, and DCMRL showed no filling of the duct after hepatic, mesenteric, or inguinal injections, indicative of primary lymphatic flow disorder (Figure 3E-I). Overall findings were consistent with GLA with central conduction abnormality. Research genetic testing of cfDNA from plasma and thoracic duct lymphatic fluid demonstrated a somatic BRAF V600E variant at 0.5% and 2.0% VAF, respectively. She is followed at an outside institution, with no further data available for review.
Discussion

This report describes six cases of CLAs associated with the pathogenic BRAF V600E variant in the absence of other known pathogenic variants. Though all six individuals had diffuse LMs and abnormal lymphatic conduction, the cases demonstrate the phenotypic heterogeneity associated with this variant and further illustrate the spectrum of morbidity associated with these disorders. To our knowledge, this is the first detailed association of the BRAF V600E with CLAs and expands the phenotypic description of this variant in patients with vascular anomalies.

The individuals described in this study underwent varied treatments, ranging from observation without intervention to dietary modification to targeted pharmacotherapies to surgical and procedural interventions. This study did not evaluate the efficacy of specific treatments in this patient population. However, our experience suggests that elucidating the genetic basis for CLAs may inform a more directed approach to treatment, especially as it relates to targeted pharmacotherapy, though additional studies are needed.

Interestingly, five of the six individuals reported in our case series developed symptoms related to abnormal lymphatic conduction only after surgical interventions. Additionally, in the majority of cases, the manifestation of this abnormal lymphatic conduction was found years after their initial diagnoses and surgeries. We are limited in our ability to determine whether these interventions may have disrupted the underlying lymphatic anatomy and caused or contributed to this abnormal conduction, or if the abnormal lymphatic conduction was an inherent aspect of these individuals' CLA phenotypes that would develop over time. Regardless, we propose added caution when considering procedural or surgical interventions in patients with CLAs, especially in the setting of a known causative BRAF V600E variant. We also emphasize the importance of regular longitudinal follow-up even for those individuals who are seemingly asymptomatic without treatment.

CLAs are a group of diseases that can be challenging to diagnose given significant overlap in clinical presentation, imaging, and histopathology. As we develop further understanding of the molecular etiology of these disorders, it is apparent that there may be significant genetic overlap as well. Identification of the causative gene variant in an individual diagnosed with a CLA may be critical to optimizing that individual's unique treatment plan.

passages.text: Long-term efficacy of migalastat in females with Fabry disease
Abstract
Background

Fabry disease is a progressive, X-linked lysosomal disorder caused by reduced or absent alpha-galactosidase A activity due to GLA variants. Females with Fabry disease often experience diagnostic delays and an underappreciated disease burden owing to their variable disease presentation and progression.
Methods

We conducted a post hoc analysis of all females from the clinical studies FACETS (NCT00925301) and ATTRACT (NCT01218659) and their open-label extensions, assessing baseline characteristics and long-term efficacy of migalastat regarding cardiac and renal function and Fabry-associated clinical events (FACEs).
Results

Overall, 60 females had a median migalastat exposure of 5.1 years. At baseline, the median age was 47 years with multiorgan involvement in 70.0% of females (>=2 organ systems: renal, cardiac, central nervous system, peripheral nervous system and gastrointestinal). At baseline, 21.7% of females had left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH). In multiorgan involvement and LVH subgroups, the median baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was in chronic kidney disease stage 2. Annualised rate of change in left ventricular mass index remained below 1 g/m2/year regardless of LVH or eGFR category at baseline. Mean (SD) eGFR annualised change was -1.1 (2.8) mL/min/1.73 m2 overall. Ten FACEs were reported in eight females, seven of whom had prior events. Seven FACEs were cardiac; the remaining three were cerebrovascular (all transient ischaemic attacks). The incidence of renal, cardiac and cerebrovascular events was 0, 24.9 and 10.7 events per 1000 patient-years, respectively.
Conclusion
These data show that females with Fabry disease experience considerable disease severity and burden and support the long-term efficacy of migalastat for the treatment of females.
WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

Fabry disease presentation and progression in females is heterogeneous, so females with Fabry disease experience diagnostic delays that may result in underappreciated disease burden and delayed treatment and management.
WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS

This post hoc analysis of females from the Phase III FACETS and ATTRACT trials, and their respective open-label extensions, challenges the perception that the burden of Fabry disease is low in females and demonstrates the benefits of migalastat treatment in this population. This analysis shows preservation of renal function across chronic kidney disease categories, reduction or maintenance of left ventricular mass index regardless of cardiac hypertrophy at baseline and a low incidence of Fabry-associated clinical events in both enzyme replacement therapy (ERT)-naive and ERT-experienced female patients. This is the largest clinical trial cohort of females with Fabry disease to date.
HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

These findings highlight the importance of assessing disease burden and treatment options in females with Fabry disease and support the long-term use and efficacy of migalastat for the treatment of females with amenable GLA variants, even in cases of multisystemic disease burden.
Introduction

Fabry disease is a rare, X-linked lysosomal disorder caused by GLA gene variants that lead to deficiency of the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A (alpha-Gal A). Reduced or absent alpha-Gal A results in the progressive accumulation of glycosphingolipids in multiple tissues of the body. This accumulation results in organ system dysfunction, most significantly, in the renal, cardiac and nervous systems. Fabry-associated clinical events (FACEs), especially related to these three organ systems, are a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with Fabry disease .

Owing to its X-linked inheritance, females with Fabry disease are often incorrectly referred to as 'carriers' of the condition; therefore, clinical investigations have mainly focused on Fabry disease in males. However, it is now well recognised that Fabry disease progression in females is heterogeneous in both timing and organ systems involved. In females with Fabry disease, impairment of renal, cardiac and cerebrovascular organ systems may start later and progress at a lower rate than in males, but it often results in multiorgan involvement over time. There is a wide spectrum of phenotypic presentations of Fabry disease that range from mild to severe; involvement of at least two major organ systems is associated with the severe Fabry phenotype. Because of heterogeneous disease presentation and later onset for many signs and symptoms, female patients experience diagnostic delays that can be substantial and extend over a decade or more. Diagnostic delays and infrequent monitoring of disease progression can result in delayed treatment and the disease burden being overlooked in females who meet the criteria for Fabry-specific treatment.

passages.text: Approved treatment for Fabry disease includes infused recombinant enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with agalsidase alfa, agalsidase beta or pegunigalsidase alfa, or migalastat, for patients with amenable variants. Migalastat is a first-in-class oral pharmacologic chaperone with broad tissue distribution and is not associated with immunogenicity. Migalastat selectively and reversibly binds to wild-type as well as certain mutant forms of alpha-Gal A, the genotypes of which are termed amenable variants. Data from the migalastat Phase III clinical programme (ATTRACT, FACETS) have shown multisystemic benefits of migalastat in patients with Fabry disease who have amenable GLA variants. Both males and females showed stabilised renal function, decreased cardiac mass and low incidence of FACEs during migalastat treatment for up to 30 months in these studies.

The current post hoc analysis of females from the Phase III FACETS and ATTRACT trials aimed to better understand the spectrum of disease severity and examine the long-term efficacy of migalastat in females with Fabry disease. These trials were the first long-term studies of migalastat and the first controlled trials in Fabry disease to include meaningful representation of females. Females assessed were enrolled in the FACETS and ATTRACT trials and their respective open-label extension (OLE) studies. Figure 1 provides a summary of the analysis as a graphical abstract.

Methods
Study design and patients

This post hoc analysis integrated data collected from female patients who participated in the Phase III clinical trials of migalastat: FACETS, ATTRACT and their OLE studies. The detailed study methodology has been published previously; an overview of the study methodology is provided here.

Patients enrolled in the randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled FACETS study received either 123 mg double-blind migalastat or placebo every other day for 6 months, followed by 18 months of open-label migalastat. Based on prior exposure to ERT, patients were enrolled in the randomised, open-label, active-controlled ATTRACT study and received open-label migalastat or open-label ERT for 18 months, followed by 12 months of open-label migalastat. Full details of study enrolment have been published previously. On completion of the FACETS and ATTRACT studies, patients could enrol in the OLE studies AT1001-041 and AT1001-042 for up to 5 years. The study design is outlined in online supplemental figure S1.

Patients in the FACETS study were considered eligible if they had never received ERT or had discontinued ERT for >=6 months prior to enrolment and had urine globotriaosylceramide (GL-3) at least four times the upper limit of normal; these patients were termed 'ERT naive'. Patients in the ATTRACT study were termed 'ERT experienced' and were eligible to enrol if they had initiated ERT>=12 months before study entry. In both pivotal studies, patients were 16-74 years of age with genetically confirmed Fabry disease and had GLA variants that were considered amenable to migalastat treatment. Female patients represented 61.9% of patients in the migalastat Phase III clinical trial programme. This is the largest number of female Fabry patients studied in a clinical programme to date and is representative of the expected proportion of female:male individuals with a GLA variant (per Mendelian inheritance).
Assessments
Renal function

Renal involvement was investigated in a subpopulation of female patients, all of whom had >=2 years of migalastat exposure (n=47). Renal function measures included annualised rate of change in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), assessed using the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration equation (eGFRCKD-EPI), and 24-hour urine protein; both were evaluated at baseline and every 6 months through to completion of the study. Detailed methods have been previously published.
Left ventricular mass index (LVMi)

Females entering the study were evaluated using echocardiography at baseline, and LVMi was assessed through blinded centralised evaluation of echocardiographic images taken at scheduled visits during the study period. Baseline LVMi was used to assess left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) status. The evolution of cardiac involvement was evaluated using the annualised rate of change in LVMi. For patients entering the OLE study AT1001-041, the baseline visit was used as the last assessment for the preceding clinical trial. For patients entering the OLE study AT1001-042, a baseline echocardiogram (ECHO) was conducted for patients who had not had an ECHO within the previous 6 months.
Fabry-associated clinical events (FACEs)

FACEs have been defined previously and include the following: (1) renal events, including doubling of serum creatinine level from the start of baseline (where levels remained double or greater between two consecutive visits) or the need for long-term dialysis or transplantation; (2) cardiac events, including myocardial infarction, new symptomatic arrhythmia requiring medication, direct current cardioversion or interventional procedure (eg, ablation, pacemakers or defibrillator implantation), unstable angina defined by national practice guidelines and accompanied by ECG changes resulting in hospitalisation, or congestive heart failure requiring hospitalisation; (3) cerebrovascular events, including stroke (documented by a physician), transient ischaemic attack (TIA; documented by a physician) or death due to FACEs (recorded based on the FACE category). The baseline for all FACEs was defined as the start of migalastat treatment. Events captured prior to enrolment in FACETS or ATTRACT were not defined using the FACE definitions and instead were events that were deemed by the treating physician to be relevant and significant to Fabry disease. These events were entered in the study record as 'prior events'.
Statistical analysis

Analyses were performed on all patients with amenable variants who were treated with migalastat. Subgroup analysis was performed on patients with multiorgan (defined as involvement of >=2 organ systems) or non-multiorgan (defined as no organ involvement or <2 organ systems involved) involvement of the following organ systems: renal, cardiac, central nervous, peripheral nervous and gastrointestinal. Involvement of an organ system was based on a medical chart review of physician-reported dictionary-derived terms using medical history, as well as eGFR<90 mL/min/1.73 m2, proteinuria>500 mg/24 hours recorded in the medical history or at baseline and LVMi>95 g/m2 at baseline. Subgroup analysis was also performed on patients with LVH (LVMi>95 g/m2) and without LVH (LVMi<=95 g/m2). Descriptive statistics for categorical variables were summarised by frequency and percentage. Continuous variables were used for efficacy analysis and were summarised using mean, SD, median, minimum, maximum and IQR.

Annualised rate of change in eGFR by eGFRCKD-EPI was calculated using simple linear regression. Individual rates of change were grouped by the extent of organ system involvement (multiorgan/non-multiorgan) and baseline eGFRCKD-EPI (>30 to <60, 60-90 and >90 mL/min/1.73 m2), or urinary protein (<300, 300-1000 and >1000 mg/24 hours). Change in LVMi was evaluated using simple linear regression based on observed values and assessment times overall and stratified by baseline eGFRCKD-EPI category (30 to <60, 60-90 and >90 mL/min/1.73 m2) or urinary protein category (<300, 300-1000 and >1000 mg/24 hours).

A mixed model for repeated measures was used to study the relationship between changes in eGFR and LVMi over time. The following covariates were used in the model: age, eGFR, LVMi and urine protein at the start of migalastat treatment, time from diagnosis, age at the start of migalastat treatment and two binary predictors (ERT status (ERT experienced vs ERT naive) and multiorgan versus non-multiorgan involvement).
Incidence of FACEs was calculated as events per 1000 patient-years, with time to first FACE assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis.
Results
Baseline characteristics

In total, 97 patients from two Phase III studies, FACETS and ATTRACT, and their respective OLE studies were included in the integrated data set for analysis, of whom 60 were female. In the overall population, median migalastat exposure in the 60 female patients was 5.1 years, ranging from 1 month to 8.5 years. Female patients had a mean (SD) age of 46.6 (12.6) years at migalastat initiation, with a median (range) time since diagnosis of 6.0 (3.0, 16.0) years.
Characteristics of female patients by multiorgan involvement

Post hoc analyses of this population of female patients were performed based on the involvement of >=2 organ systems (multiorgan) or <2 organ systems (non-multiorgan) at baseline (table 1). There were 42 females with multiorgan involvement and 18 females with non-multiorgan involvement at baseline. Of females with multiorgan involvement, 74% were older than 40 years of age; they were generally older than those with non-multiorgan involvement (median (25th percentile (Q1), 75th percentile (Q3)) 48.5 (40.0, 58.0) vs 41.0 (31.0, 51.0) years, respectively). At baseline, females with multiorgan involvement had a median (Q1, Q3) eGFRCKD-EPI of 88.9 (74.7, 107.0) mL/min/1.73 m2 and urinary protein levels indicated microalbuminuria (201 mg/24 hours), reflective of mild kidney disease. In females with non-multiorgan involvement, median eGFRCKD-EPI was 108.5 mL/min/1.73 m2 and urinary protein levels indicated lower levels of microalbuminuria (106.5 mg/24 hours). Females with multiorgan involvement had a higher median (Q1, Q3) LVMi at baseline (81.6 (71.2, 94.1) g/m2) than females with non-multiorgan involvement (73.5 (65.4, 85.2) g/m2; table 1). More females with multiorgan involvement were receiving ACE inhibitors (ACEIs)/angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs)/renin inhibitors (RIs) than females with non-multiorgan involvement (n=19, 45.2% vs n=6, 33.3%, respectively; table 1).

Characteristics of female patients by baseline LVH

Of the 60 females in this overall population, 13 (21.7%) had LVH at baseline (LVMi>95 g/m2; table 2). Females with LVH were generally older than those without LVH (mean age 54.0 vs 45.5 years) and had less-preserved renal function (eGFRCKD-EPI 78.5 vs 97.7 mL/min/1.72 m2). Most females with LVH also had renal impairment; 69.2% of patients with LVH at baseline had mild renal impairment (eGFR 60-90 mL/min/1.73 m2; table 2). Females without LVH were less likely to have received ACEI/ARB/RI treatment than those with LVH at baseline (table 2).
