passages.text: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)

SAH is characterized by bleeding into the subarachnoid space:the area between the arachnoid and pia mater that contains typically cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). The most common cause of non-traumatic SAH is the rupture of an intracranial saccular (berry) aneurysm, typically located at arterial bifurcations in the circle of Willis. Other etiologies include AVMs, trauma, coagulopathies, and, less commonly, cortical vein thrombosis or vasculitis. Upon rupture of an aneurysm, high-pressure arterial blood is forcefully ejected into the subarachnoid space, rapidly increasing ICP and causing a sudden, severe headache often described as a "thunderclap headache". The blood mixes with CSF, spreads over the cortical surface and basal cisterns, and may enter the ventricular system. The initial mechanical effect includes a transient rise in ICP, which reduces cerebral perfusion pressure, resulting in global cerebral ischemia or even loss of consciousness. Additionally, hemolysis of the extravasated blood releases oxyhemoglobin, a potent irritant that initiates vasospasm of cerebral arteries, typically peaking between 4 and 14 days post-hemorrhage. Vasospasm leads to delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI), a major contributor to morbidity and poor outcomes in SAH survivors. Inflammatory responses are triggered by the presence of blood and its breakdown products, activating microglia and astrocytes and leading to cytokine production, oxidative damage, and BBB dysfunction. Inflammatory molecules such as IL-6, MCP-1, and MMPs contribute to secondary injury and cerebral edema. Moreover, SAH may induce hydrocephalus by obstructing CSF circulation at the level of arachnoid granulations or ventricles, further elevating ICP. Many genetic variants have been reported to be associated with SAH. Mutations in the COL3A1 and TGFBR2 genes, both of which affect the structural integrity of the vascular wall, are associated with aneurysm formation and rupture. These mutations weaken blood vessels, making them more susceptible to rupture under pressure.
Genetic associations with different stroke types are discussed in the next section in detail.
Genetic risk factors for stroke
Common genetic variants identified through genome-wide association studies

Over the past decade, genome-wide association studies have revolutionized our understanding of the genetic architecture of complex diseases, including stroke (Fig. 1). Unlike candidate gene studies that focus on specific hypotheses, GWAS scans the entire genome for single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that are more frequently present in individuals with a disease than in healthy controls. These studies have been particularly valuable for stroke, a heterogeneous condition influenced by multiple genes and environmental factors. To date, GWAS has identified over 30 genetic loci associated with different forms of stroke, including both ischemic and hemorrhagic subtypes. These loci often implicate genes involved in vascular biology, inflammation, endothelial function, lipid metabolism, and cardiac electrophysiology (Fig. 2). Importantly, many of these associations are subtype-specific, reflecting the distinct etiopathologies of large-artery atherosclerosis, small vessel disease, cardioembolic stroke, and ICH (Table 1).
Some of the most consistently replicated and biologically plausible loci identified by GWAS are discussed below.
Histone deacetylase 9

HDAC9, located on chromosome 7p21.1, is among the most consistently replicated loci associated with large-artery atherosclerotic stroke (LAA) in GWAS. As a member of the class IIa histone deacetylase family, HDAC9 plays a pivotal role in epigenetic regulation of gene expression by removing acetyl groups from lysine residues on histones, leading to chromatin condensation and transcriptional repression. In the vascular context, HDAC9 regulates key processes, including vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, monocyte/macrophage activation, and inflammatory signaling. It has been identified in multiple GWAS as a susceptibility gene for LAA; particularly, the SNPs rs11984041 and rs2107595 are strongly associated with this stroke subtype. The risk allele of rs2107595 correlates with increased expression of HDAC9 mRNA in carotid atherosclerotic plaques, suggesting a functional consequence. Functionally, HDAC9 promotes vascular inflammation by enhancing NF-kappaB signaling. It deacetylates IKKalpha and IKKbeta, leading to activation of downstream inflammatory pathways and upregulation of cytokines such as TNF-alpha and IL-6. Its overexpression in plaques has been linked to increased macrophage infiltration, extracellular matrix degradation, and plaque destabilization, features that enhance the risk of thromboembolic events and ischemic stroke. Experimental evidence supports a pathogenic role, as HDAC9 knockdown in murine models results in reduced atherosclerotic lesion formation, decreased inflammatory gene expression, and improved vascular function. Moreover, cis-regulatory elements at the HDAC9 locus have been shown to modulate its expression in human atheroprone tissues, adding an epigenetic layer of control to its genetic associations. Given this mechanistic profile, HDAC9 has emerged as a promising therapeutic target. While non-selective HDAC inhibitors are already in clinical use for other conditions, selective HDAC9 inhibition is being explored as a potential precision strategy to reduce vascular inflammation and plaque burden without systemic toxicity.

passages.text: Paired-like homeodomain transcription factor 2 and zinc finger homeobox 3

Cardioembolic stroke (CE), which arises from emboli originating in the heart, is most frequently caused by atrial fibrillation (AF). GWAS of both AF and cardioembolic stroke have consistently implicated two key loci: PITX2 and ZFHX3. PITX2, located on chromosome 4q25, encodes a homeobox transcription factor essential for left-right asymmetry in embryonic development and electrophysiological regulation of atrial cardiomyocytes. Variants such as rs2200733 and rs10033464 are significantly associated with AF and, by extension, with an increased risk of cardioembolic stroke. The gene appears to modulate atrial electrical remodeling, predisposing to arrhythmogenesis. ZFHX3 (zinc finger homeobox 3), located on chromosome 16q22, is another transcription factor involved in cardiac ion channel regulation. SNPs like rs2106261 have been linked to both AF and cardioembolic stroke risk. ZFHX3 influences the atrial structure and conduction properties, and its dysregulation has been implicated in atrial fibrosis and inflammation. These two genes are now incorporated into polygenic risk scores for AF and are being evaluated as markers to guide long-term anticoagulation in stroke prevention.
Nerve injury-induced protein 2

The NINJ2 gene, located on chromosome 12p13, encodes a cell surface adhesion molecule expressed primarily in endothelial cells and Schwann cells. It was initially identified as a susceptibility locus for ischemic stroke in a GWAS by the CHARGE consortium, which reported a significant association between two single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) (rs11833579 and rs12425791) and increased stroke risk, particularly in older adults. The study found that carriers of the risk alleles had a 1.3-1.4-fold higher risk of ischemic stroke, marking one of the first GWAS-identified loci for this complex disease. Functionally, NINJ2 has been implicated in nerve regeneration, endothelial inflammation, and vascular injury response. In vitro studies have shown that NINJ2 expression is upregulated under inflammatory stimuli and promotes endothelial cell activation through TLR4/NF-kappaB and c-Jun signaling, resulting in the increased production of VCAM-1, IL-6, and other pro-inflammatory mediators. Although NINJ2 has been proposed to contribute to BBB integrity, direct in vivo evidence demonstrating a causal role in BBB maintenance or repair after stroke remains lacking. While some speculative connections have been drawn based on its role in endothelial adhesion and inflammation, these mechanistic pathways have not yet been fully validated in stroke models. The suggestion of NINJ2's role in post-stroke BBB repair should, therefore, be interpreted cautiously and warrants further experimental investigation. Since its initial identification, replication of the NINJ2-stroke association has been inconsistent across populations. Some studies have supported the association of rs12425791 with ischemic stroke, while rs11833579 has failed to replicate in multiple independent cohorts. This variability suggests potential gene-environment interactions or ancestry-specific effects, though these have yet to be formally demonstrated. In summary, while NINJ2 remains a gene of tentative interest in stroke biology due to its initial GWAS association and involvement in vascular inflammatory signaling, its precise role in stroke pathophysiology, BBB repair, or neurovascular recovery remains to be conclusively established. Future studies focusing on in vivo validation, regulatory mechanisms, and population-specific effects are needed to clarify the relevance of NINJ2 in cerebrovascular disease. Other GWAS-Linked Stroke Genes Beyond these core loci, several other genes identified in large multi-ancestry GWAS and meta-analyses contribute to our understanding of stroke susceptibility. Subsequent studies across multiple ancestries showed inconsistent replication, and the causal mechanism remains uncertain.
Collagen alpha-1(IV) chain (COL4A1)/Collagen alpha-2(IV) chain (COL4A2)

The COL4A1 and COL4A2 genes, located on chromosome 13q34, encode the alpha1 and alpha2 chains of type IV collagen, respectively. These chains assemble into heterotrimers that are integral components of the vascular basement membrane, providing structural support to the cerebral microvasculature, particularly small perforating arteries that are susceptible to damage in stroke. Pathogenic variants in COL4A1 and COL4A2 have been linked to monogenic forms of cerebral SVD. Clinical manifestations include porencephaly, leukoencephalopathy, lacunar infarctions, deep ICH, and ocular and renal anomalies. These mutations often result in systemic vascular fragility syndromes. GWAS have identified common intronic variants in COL4A2 associated with increased risk of deep ICH and lacunar ischemic stroke. While these associations are statistically significant, they exhibit modest effect sizes and require further replication across diverse populations. Mutations in COL4A1/COL4A2 disrupt the assembly and secretion of type IV collagen, compromising basement membrane integrity. This leads to endothelial dysfunction, increased BBB permeability, and heightened susceptibility to microvascular rupture or occlusion. Experimental models have demonstrated that these mutations impair angiogenesis, alter pericyte-endothelial interactions, and promote BBB dysfunction, culminating in microbleeds and progressive ischemia. In sporadic stroke cases, carriers of COL4A1/2 variants exhibit an elevated risk for both deep hemorrhagic and lacunar ischemic strokes, suggesting a shared genetic etiology underlying microangiopathy. This challenges the traditional dichotomy between ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke subtypes, highlighting a continuum of small vessel pathology. Genetic screening for COL4A1/2 mutations is increasingly considered in younger patients with atypical stroke presentations, especially when imaging reveals white matter changes or recurrent deep infarcts and hemorrhages (; "The expanding phenotype of COL4A1 and COL4A2 mutations," 2015, p. 1). Understanding the role of COL4A1/2 in vascular integrity has spurred interest in developing targeted therapies. Potential strategies include promoting protein folding, ECM-related proteins such as MMPs, and interventions aimed at preserving BBB function. While these approaches are promising, they remain under investigation, and further research is necessary to translate these findings into clinical practice.
LPA (lipoprotein(a))

The LPA gene encodes lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)], an LDL-like particle distinguished by the presence of apolipoprotein(a), which is covalently bound to apolipoprotein B-100. Elevated circulating levels of Lp(a) have long been implicated in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. More recently, genetic studies have linked LPA variants to large artery ischemic stroke, particularly those arising from atherosclerotic plaque formation in major extracranial and intracranial vessels. The atherogenic and pro-thrombotic properties of Lp(a) arise from both its lipid-rich core, which contributes to cholesterol deposition in arterial walls, and its apolipoprotein(a) component, which structurally resembles plasminogen. This molecular mimicry allows Lp (a) to interfere with fibrinolysis, thereby impairing clot resolution and promoting thrombosis. Lp(a) also acts as a pro-inflammatory mediator, promoting endothelial dysfunction, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and vascular smooth muscle proliferation:all hallmarks of atherogenesis and plaque instability.
1q22 locus (e.g., PMF1, SLC25A44)

The 1q22 locus, encompassing genes such as PMF1 and SLC25A44, has been identified through GWAS as a significant susceptibility region for non-lobar intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), a subtype of stroke often associated with hypertension and cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD). In a meta-analysis conducted by Woo et al., the single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) rs2984613, located intronically within PMF1, demonstrated a strong association with non-lobar ICH (odds ratio [OR] 1.44; p = 1.6 x 10-8), while showing no significant association with lobar ICH. Subsequent deep resequencing studies of the 1q22 region have provided further insights. These studies identified both common and rare variants within the SEMA4A 5'-untranslated region (UTR) and the PMF1 intronic regions, which overlap with the active promoter and enhancer elements, suggesting potential regulatory roles. Chromatin conformation analyses, utilizing techniques such as Hi-C and ChIA-PET, revealed that 1q22 is organized within a single topologically associating domain (TAD), facilitating long-range interactions between the SEMA4A promoter and PMF1 enhancer regions. Multivariable Mendelian randomization analyses indicated that increased expression of PMF1 may be causally related to an elevated risk of non-lobar ICH. These findings underscore the importance of regulatory mechanisms at the 1q22 locus in the pathogenesis of non-lobar ICH. The involvement of PMF1 and SLC25A44 in vascular integrity and function suggests that dysregulation at this locus could contribute to the vulnerability of small cerebral vessels to hemorrhage, particularly under hypertensive conditions.
SH2B3, ABO, and ALDH2

The SH2B3 gene, also known as LNK, encodes an adaptor protein involved in regulating hematopoiesis, inflammation, and vascular homeostasis. Genetic variants in SH2B3 have been associated with various cardiovascular diseases, including stroke. Specifically, the missense variant rs3184504 has been linked to an increased risk of ischemic stroke. This variant is thought to influence vascular inflammation and endothelial function, contributing to atherosclerotic processes.

The ABO gene determines an individual's blood group (A, B, AB, or O) and has been implicated in stroke risk. Studies have shown that individuals with non-O blood types, particularly type A, have a higher risk of ischemic stroke compared to those with blood type O. This increased risk is attributed to higher levels of von Willebrand factor and factor VIII in non-O individuals, which can promote thrombosis. Meta-analyses indicate that individuals with blood group A have a higher risk of ischemic stroke, particularly early onset, whereas group O is associated with a lower risk, consistent with higher vWF/Factor VIII levels in non-O groups and cohort findings from REGARDS.

The ALDH2 gene encodes the mitochondrial enzyme aldehyde dehydrogenase 2, which is crucial for metabolizing toxic aldehydes such as acetaldehyde and 4-hydroxynonenal. The rs671 polymorphism, also known as ALDH2*2, involves a G-to-A nucleotide substitution, resulting in a glutamate-to-lysine amino acid change at position 504. This mutation significantly reduces the enzymatic activity of ALDH2, leading to the accumulation of harmful aldehydes that can cause vascular endothelial damage and promote inflammation. A comprehensive meta-analysis identified a significant association between the ALDH2 rs671 variant and increased risk of ischemic stroke, particularly in East Asian populations. Notably, this association exhibited sex-specific effects, with the strongest correlation observed in males. This finding underscores the importance of considering genetic background and sex in stroke risk assessments. Beyond stroke, the rs671 polymorphism has been linked to other cardiovascular conditions. For instance, individuals with the A/A genotype have shown a higher susceptibility to coronary artery disease and hemorrhagic stroke. This increased risk is attributed to the variant's role in promoting oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction. Interestingly, the rs671 variant also appears to influence blood pressure regulation. Some studies suggest that carriers of the A allele may have a reduced prevalence of hypertension, particularly in individuals with lower metabolic risk profiles. This protective effect is thought to be mediated through mechanisms involving reduced oxidative stress and improved vascular function. Therefore, ALDH2 rs671 polymorphism plays a multifaceted role in cardiovascular health, influencing susceptibility to ischemic stroke, coronary artery disease, and hypertension. Its effects are modulated by genetic background, sex, and metabolic status, highlighting the need for personalized approaches in risk assessment and management.
TGFBR2

Transforming Growth Factor Beta Receptor 2 (TGFBR2) encodes a serine/threonine kinase receptor involved in the TGF-beta signaling pathway, which plays a central role in vascular development, extracellular matrix regulation, and immune modulation. Variants and mutations in TGFBR2 have been associated with increased susceptibility to hemorrhagic stroke, particularly SAH due to intracranial aneurysm rupture. Inherited disorders such as Loeys-Dietz syndrome, caused by pathogenic mutations in TGFBR2, are characterized by vascular fragility and predisposition to arterial aneurysms, dissections, and early-onset stroke. The structural instability of cerebral vessels in affected individuals reflects impaired collagen synthesis, dysregulated TGF-beta signaling, and inflammatory remodeling of the vascular wall. Even in the absence of syndromic features, polymorphisms in TGFBR2 have been implicated in aneurysmal disease and cerebrovascular vulnerability. Studies have shown altered TGFBR2 expression in aneurysmal tissues, supporting its role in the pathogenesis of SAH. These findings position TGFBR2 as both a genetic risk locus and a potential therapeutic target in the context of stroke subtypes linked to vessel wall integrity and aneurysmal rupture.
MTHFR

The MTHFR (methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase) gene encodes an enzyme crucial for folate metabolism and the regulation of homocysteine levels in the blood. One of the most widely studied polymorphisms in this gene, C677T (rs1801133), results in a thermolabile variant of the enzyme with reduced activity, leading to elevated plasma homocysteine:a known risk factor for vascular endothelial dysfunction and thrombotic events. Numerous studies have demonstrated that individuals homozygous for the T allele (TT genotype) have a significantly increased risk of stroke, particularly in populations with low dietary folate intake. Elevated homocysteine promotes oxidative stress, endothelial injury, and a pro-inflammatory, pro-thrombotic environment that predisposes to cerebrovascular events. Although the strength of the association varies by ethnicity and environmental factors, meta-analyses have consistently linked the MTHFR C677T polymorphism to both large-artery and small-vessel ischemic strokes. Effect sizes vary by ancestry and folate status, and large cohorts/Mendelian-randomization analyses often report attenuated or null associations where folate intake is sufficient. Another variant, A1298C, has also been explored, although its impact on enzyme activity and stroke risk appears to be significant in some studies, others didn't report any effect on stroke predisposition. While homocysteine-lowering therapies using folic acid and B vitamins have shown mixed results in stroke prevention trials, individuals with the TT genotype may derive specific benefits from targeted nutritional interventions (Huang et al., 2024). The MTHFR gene thus represents an important example of gene-environment interaction in stroke pathophysiology, highlighting how genetic predisposition can be modulated by modifiable lifestyle and dietary factors.
ACE

The ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) gene plays a pivotal role in the renin-angiotensin system, regulating blood pressure and vascular tone by converting angiotensin I to the potent vasoconstrictor angiotensin II. A well-characterized polymorphism in the ACE gene is the insertion/deletion (I/D) variant (rs4646994), which involves the presence (insertion, I) or absence (deletion, D) of a 287-bp Alu repeat sequence in intron 16. The D allele is associated with increased circulating and tissue ACE levels, enhancing angiotensin II production and promoting vasoconstriction, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and vascular remodeling:all key processes implicated in stroke pathogenesis. Several studies and meta-analyses have linked the DD genotype to an elevated risk of ischemic stroke, particularly in hypertensive individuals, as well as to an increased risk of hemorrhagic stroke due to its role in vessel wall fragility and blood pressure regulation. The association appears to be stronger in Asian populations, possibly reflecting gene-environment interactions such as salt sensitivity and dietary patterns. Moreover, elevated ACE activity may contribute to atherosclerosis and cerebral small vessel disease, further compounding stroke susceptibility. Although the ACE I/D polymorphism is not currently used clinically for stroke risk prediction, it remains an important genetic marker in research exploring the interface between hypertension, vascular pathology, and cerebrovascular events.
Rare genetic variants and monogenic disorders

While most strokes result from complex interactions between multiple genetic variants and environmental factors, rare monogenic disorders can significantly increase stroke risk. These conditions often result in early-onset stroke or familial stroke syndromes (Table 2).
Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy

Among the rare monogenic causes of stroke, CADASIL is the most well-characterized and frequently encountered. It is caused by mutations in the NOTCH3 gene located on chromosome 19p13.2, which encodes a transmembrane receptor primarily expressed in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs). These mutations, typically involving cysteine residues within epidermal growth factor-like repeats, result in the misfolding and accumulation of the Notch3 extracellular domain in the walls of small arteries. This process leads to the formation of granular osmiophilic material (GOM) deposits, ultimately triggering degeneration of VSMCs and progressive arteriopathy. Pathologically, CADASIL is characterized by concentric thickening of the small- and medium-sized cerebral arteries, lumen narrowing, and chronic hypoperfusion of deep white matter regions. These vascular alterations underlie the clinical and radiological manifestations of the disease. Most patients begin to exhibit symptoms between the third and fifth decades of life. Clinically, CADASIL presents with migraine with aura (often an early feature), recurrent subcortical ischemic events, mood disturbances, cognitive impairment, and, eventually, vascular dementia. Cognitive symptoms usually progress slowly, initially involving executive dysfunction and processing speed before affecting memory. Genetic testing remains the gold standard for diagnosis and involves identifying pathogenic variants in the NOTCH3 gene. Over 200 mutations have been identified, and their detection enables confirmation of the diagnosis in suspected cases and predictive testing in at-risk relatives. When genetic testing yields inconclusive results, ultrastructural analysis of a skin biopsy for GOM deposits can provide additional diagnostic evidence. As a genetically determined small vessel disease, CADASIL has no known cure, and current management strategies focus on symptom control and stroke prevention. The use of antiplatelet agents remains empirically guided, while the avoidance of thrombolytics and vasoconstrictive medications is advised due to potential complications. However, a few recent reports have deemed thrombolysis safe in CADASIL. Because NOTCH3 mutations promote stroke independently of classical vascular risk factors, aggressive control of hypertension and smoking remains essential, though it does not halt disease progression. Ongoing research efforts are investigating potential disease-modifying strategies, including molecular approaches to reduce Notch3 aggregation or preserve VSMC integrity. CADASIL stands as a paradigm of how single-gene mutations can produce a clear and reproducible cerebrovascular phenotype. It underscores the critical role of genetic mechanisms in small vessel stroke, highlighting the importance of integrating genomic data with clinical, imaging, and pathological information. For neurologists and stroke specialists, early recognition of CADASIL is essential:not only for clinical management but also for genetic counseling, family screening, and inclusion in emerging targeted therapy trials.
Fabry disease

Another rare genetic cause of stroke, Fabry disease, represents a notable X-linked lysosomal storage disorder that significantly elevates stroke risk, particularly in young and middle-aged adults. The condition arises due to pathogenic variants in the GLA gene located on Xq22.1, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme alpha-galactosidase A (alpha-Gal A). Deficiency or absence of alpha-Gal A activity leads to the systemic accumulation of glycosphingolipids, particularly globotriaosylceramide (Gb3), within lysosomes of various cell types, including vascular endothelial cells, cardiomyocytes, neurons, and renal epithelial cells ("c.640-814T > C). The progressive deposition of Gb3 in the vascular endothelium results in a cascade of vascular dysfunction that underlies many of the cerebrovascular manifestations of Fabry disease. Key mechanisms include endothelial damage, oxidative stress, vascular smooth muscle proliferation, and prothrombotic alterations, all of which contribute to luminal narrowing and impaired cerebral perfusion. Importantly, Fabry disease is one of the few genetic disorders where ischemic stroke may be the presenting symptom, especially in male patients. Female heterozygotes may also experience stroke, though they often have a later onset and more variable phenotypic expression due to X-inactivation.

Cerebrovascular events in Fabry disease are primarily ischemic and often classified as cryptogenic in young patients lacking traditional vascular risk factors. Involvement of the vertebrobasilar circulation is disproportionately high compared to other stroke etiologies. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) commonly reveals white matter lesions, often confluent in the posterior circulation territory, and may also demonstrate pulvinar hyperintensities:a radiologic marker relatively specific to Fabry disease. These findings, in conjunction with a history of neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas, corneal verticillata, proteinuria, or cardiac hypertrophy, should prompt consideration of Fabry disease in young stroke patients.

Diagnosis is confirmed by an enzymatic assay measuring alpha-Gal A activity in males or by GLA gene sequencing in both sexes. Plasma globotriaosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb3) has emerged as a sensitive biomarker for disease monitoring. Early genetic diagnosis is critical as enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) and chaperone therapy has been shown to slow the progression of organ damage and may reduce the risk of stroke when initiated promptly. However, the benefit of ERT on cerebrovascular outcomes remains an area of ongoing investigation. Given its potential for early-onset stroke and systemic involvement, Fabry disease highlights the need for genetic screening in young adults with unexplained cerebrovascular events, especially in the absence of conventional risk factors. Inclusion of Fabry disease in diagnostic panels for monogenic stroke syndromes has increased, and its identification carries important implications not only for individualized therapy but also for cascade testing of at-risk family members.
Sickle cell disease (SCD)

SCD is a well-established monogenic cause of ischemic stroke, particularly in pediatric populations. It results from a missense mutation in the HBB gene (chromosome 11p15.5), specifically a single nucleotide substitution (GAG to GTG) that leads to the replacement of glutamic acid with valine at the sixth position of the beta-globin chain. This produces abnormal hemoglobin S (HbS), which polymerizes under hypoxic conditions, causing red blood cells to adopt a sickle shape. These distorted erythrocytes have reduced deformability and increased adhesiveness to the vascular endothelium, promoting microvascular occlusion and chronic vascular injury. In the cerebral vasculature, these changes are particularly detrimental, leading to intimal hyperplasia, arterial stenosis:especially in the large intracranial vessels such as the internal carotid and middle cerebral arteries:and ultimately cerebral infarction. Children with homozygous HbSS genotype are at a markedly elevated risk of both overt ischemic stroke and silent cerebral infarcts, the latter often occurring without clinical symptoms but detectable via MRI. The pathophysiological process is further compounded by chronic hemolytic anemia and systemic inflammation, which enhance endothelial dysfunction and contribute to cerebrovascular vulnerability. Genetic studies have also identified potential modifiers of stroke risk within the SCD population, including polymorphisms in genes associated with vascular tone regulation (NOS3), adhesion molecules (VCAM1), and inflammatory mediators (TNF-alpha). However, their clinical utility remains under investigation. In the context of stroke genetics, SCD exemplifies how a single point mutation can dramatically influence cerebrovascular outcomes, underscoring the importance of incorporating monogenic disorders into early risk assessment and diagnostic algorithms for stroke, particularly in young individuals.

passages.text: Polygenic risk scores (PRS)

PRS represents an emerging genomic tool that quantifies an individual's inherited predisposition to disease by aggregating the effects of thousands:or even millions:of common genetic variants, each contributing a small effect size. In the context of stroke, PRS are constructed using GWAS data that have identified numerous single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with different stroke subtypes, including large artery atherosclerotic stroke, small vessel disease, and cardioembolic stroke. While no single SNP confers high risk in isolation, the cumulative burden of risk alleles can stratify individuals into different risk categories.

Recent large-scale studies, including those from the MEGASTROKE consortium and UK Biobank, have shown that individuals in the top decile of PRS for ischemic stroke exhibit a 2-3 fold higher lifetime risk of stroke compared to those in the lowest decile, independent of traditional risk factors such as age, hypertension, diabetes, or smoking. Importantly, these scores are particularly valuable for early risk prediction in asymptomatic individuals, including younger populations or those with a family history of stroke, where conventional risk calculators may fall short.

Moreover, stroke-specific PRS have demonstrated subtype selectivity. For instance, PRS derived from atrial fibrillation-associated SNPs correlate strongly with cardioembolic stroke risk, while others enriched for atherosclerotic markers associate more with large artery stroke. This has led to the development of subtype-specific meta GRS (meta-genomic risk scores), which combine multiple stroke-related traits and improve predictive accuracy. Integrating PRS into clinical practice could potentially enable the development of tailored preventive strategies:such as earlier intervention, intensified lifestyle modification, or targeted screening:in high-risk individuals.

Despite their promise, challenges remain before PRS can be widely implemented in stroke care. These include population-specific calibration (as most PRS are derived from European ancestry cohorts), standardization of scoring algorithms, and the integration of PRS into existing clinical workflows. Nevertheless, as genomic datasets diversify and predictive algorithms become more robust, PRS holds considerable potential to transform stroke risk assessment by enabling precision prevention and early personalized intervention.
Functional genomics and stroke
Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and disease modeling

Functional genomics has revolutionized our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying stroke and related cerebrovascular disorders. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), reprogrammed from patient-specific somatic cells, provide a versatile platform to model stroke-associated genetic mutations. These iPSCs can differentiate into various cell types pertinent to stroke pathology, including neurons, endothelial cells, and VSMCs, enabling the recreation of the brain's microenvironment during ischemic events.
Modeling monogenic stroke disorders
CADASIL and NOTCH3 mutations.

As previously discussed, CADASIL is primarily caused by mutations in the NOTCH3 gene. iPSC-derived models from CADASIL patients have been instrumental in elucidating the disease's pathophysiology (Wang et al., 2025). Studies have shown that these mutations lead to the degeneration of VSMCs and impair neurovascular interactions, contributing to BBB dysfunction.
COL4A1/A2 mutations and small vessel disease.

We discussed how the mutations in COL4A1 and COL4A2 genes are implicated in cerebral small vessel disease (SVD), a significant cause of stroke and dementia. iPSC-derived co-culture models of mural and endothelial cells from patients with these mutations have revealed that the mutations induce apoptosis, migration defects, and extracellular matrix remodeling in mural cells. These pathological changes adversely affect endothelial cell tight junctions, compromising BBB integrity. Notably, inhibition of MMPs in these models has shown partial restoration of normal cellular functions, suggesting potential therapeutic avenues.
Blood-brain barrier modeling.

iPSC-derived brain microvascular endothelial cells (iPSC-BMECs) have been developed to study BBB properties in vitro. These models have demonstrated that neurovascular interactions enhance BBB function. However, in the context of CADASIL, mural cells derived from patients fail to support these interactions effectively, leading to compromised barrier integrity. CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing in Stroke Research
The advent of CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing technology has provided researchers with precise tools to investigate the functional consequences of specific genetic variants associated with stroke.
Functional studies of stroke-related genes
HDAC9 and COL4A1.

As discussed earlier, variants in the HDAC9 gene have been linked to an increased risk of large artery stroke. Utilizing CRISPR/Cas9, researchers have introduced or corrected mutations in HDAC9 and COL4A1 within iPSC-derived models to study their roles in vascular health and stroke susceptibility. These models have facilitated the dissection of molecular pathways involved in stroke pathogenesis and the identification of potential therapeutic targets. Despite strong genetic links between HDAC9 and large-artery atherosclerotic stroke, several issues temper translation of HDAC-targeted therapies. First, selectivity remains limited: available inhibitors often target multiple isoforms, which may blunt pro-inflammatory signaling but also disrupt neuroplasticity and hematopoiesis. Second, pharmacokinetics and blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration are challenging; achieving plaque- and brain-relevant exposure without systemic toxicity is difficult owing to protein binding and efflux transporters. Third, the post-ischemic window is narrow, interactions with thrombolysis/antiplatelets and risk of hemorrhagic transformation warrant careful evaluation. Fourth, epigenetic adaptation may blunt durability, with potential rebound on withdrawal, implying a need for chronic dosing with uncertain long-term safety. Finally, patient heterogeneity matters: the HDAC9 signal is strongest for large-artery disease; genotype/biomarker enrichment and pharmacodynamic readouts (histone acetylation signatures, cytokines) should be embedded in trials. Table 4 summarizes the HDAC9-inflammation-BBB axis, mapping key pathway nodes (NF-kappaB activation, MMP-9-mediated matrix injury, leukocyte adhesion, and COL4A1/2-related basement-membrane fragility) to blood-brain barrier effects and stroke outcomes.

passages.text: GLA mutations and Fabry disease.

We discussed that Fabry disease, resulting from mutations in the GLA gene, is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder that can lead to stroke. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of GLA in human cell lines has been employed to create in vitro models of Fabry disease. These models have been used to study the pharmacokinetics of enzyme replacement therapies and to screen for compounds that enhance therapeutic efficacy.
Therapeutic potential of gene editing.

Beyond modeling, CRISPR/Cas9 holds promise for therapeutic interventions in monogenic stroke disorders. For instance, correcting NOTCH3 mutations in CADASIL or GLA mutations in Fabry disease using gene-editing techniques could potentially prevent stroke in individuals at high genetic risk. While clinical application remains in the early stages, preclinical studies suggest that gene therapy could become a valuable tool in stroke prevention.
Epigenetics and stroke

Epigenetic modifications are heritable changes in gene expression that do not involve alterations to the underlying DNA sequence and play pivotal roles in the pathogenesis, progression, and recovery of stroke. These modifications encompass DNA methylation, histone modifications, and the regulatory functions of non-coding RNAs, including miRNAs and long non-coding RNAs. Understanding these mechanisms offers insights into potential therapeutic targets and biomarkers for stroke (Table 5).
DNA methylation and histone modifications
DNA methylation

DNA methylation, which typically involves the addition of a methyl group to the 5-carbon of cytosine residues within CpG dinucleotides, plays a key role in the regulation of gene expression, often leading to gene silencing. In the context of stroke, aberrant DNA methylation patterns have been implicated in both the pathogenesis and progression of the disease. For instance, hypermethylation of the endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) gene promoter has been associated with reduced eNOS expression, leading to impaired vasodilation and an increased risk of ischemic events. Conversely, hypomethylation of pro-inflammatory genes can intensify the inflammatory response following a stroke, thereby exacerbating neuronal injury and contributing to unfavorable outcomes. Additionally, global DNA methylation profiles are modulated by various environmental factors such as diet, smoking, and psychological stress, each of which is recognized as a modifiable risk factor for stroke. DNA methylation modifies cytosine residues in CpG dinucleotides to regulate chromatin accessibility and transcription. At promoters and enhancers, hypermethylation generally represses gene expression whereas hypomethylation can de-repress pathways that drive vascular inflammation and thrombosis. Recent epigenome-wide analyses have linked differential methylation at loci involved in endothelial function, inflammation, and extracellular-matrix remodeling with incident stroke and with post-stroke outcomes. Acute blood DNA methylation profiles correlate with infarct size, early neurologic deterioration, and functional recovery, suggesting prognostic utility. Because DNA methylation is dynamic:TET-mediated demethylation and DNMT-driven remethylation occur over days to weeks, environmental exposures and aging can reshape neurovascular gene programs. Methodological constraints (cell-type heterogeneity, batch effects, and under-representation of diverse ancestries) remain important for replication and translation.

Therapeutically, DNMT inhibitors and dietary one-carbon donors (e. g., folate/B-vitamins) have been explored to modulate vascular risk, but broad-spectrum epigenetic agents can affect thousands of loci. Defining safe intervention windows relative to ischemia-reperfusion and integrating methylome with transcriptome/proteome readouts will be critical next steps.
Histone modifications

Histone modifications, which involve post-translational changes to histone proteins around which DNA is wrapped, play a crucial role in regulating chromatin structure and gene expression. Among these, histone acetylation, catalyzed by histone acetyltransferases, generally promotes gene transcription by relaxing the chromatin architecture, thereby allowing transcriptional machinery better access to DNA. In contrast, histone deacetylases (HDACs) remove acetyl groups, resulting in chromatin condensation and subsequent gene repression. Notably, inhibition of specific HDACs such as HDAC9 has shown neuroprotective effects in stroke models, as it enhances the expression of genes linked to neuronal survival and plasticity.

In addition to acetylation, histone methylation also plays a pivotal role in transcriptional regulation, with its impact dependent on the specific amino acid residues modified. For example, trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4me3) is associated with transcriptional activation, whereas trimethylation at lysine 27 (H3K27me3) is typically linked to gene silencing. Ischemic brain tissues exhibit altered patterns of these histone methylation marks, which in turn affect the expression of genes involved in key processes such as inflammation and apoptosis.
Non-coding RNAs

Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) represent a diverse group of RNA molecules that do not encode proteins but play essential regulatory roles in gene expression. These include microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and circular RNAs, each influencing transcriptional, post-transcriptional, and epigenetic processes. In the context of stroke, ncRNAs have emerged as critical mediators of pathophysiological responses, including inflammation, apoptosis, angiogenesis, and BBB integrity. Their tissue-specific expression, dynamic regulation during ischemia-reperfusion injury, and stability in biofluids make them not only mechanistic contributors to stroke pathology but also promising candidates for biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Recent studies have revealed that specific ncRNAs can modulate stroke outcomes by targeting key molecular pathways, thereby offering new opportunities for individualized diagnostics and interventions in stroke care.
MicroRNAs (miRNAs)

miRNAs are short (~22 nucleotides), evolutionarily conserved, non-coding RNA molecules that post-transcriptionally regulate gene expression. They exert their function primarily by binding to the 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of target mRNAs, resulting in translational repression or mRNA degradation, thereby modulating protein output without altering the underlying genetic code. A single miRNA can regulate multiple mRNA targets, and conversely, a single gene can be regulated by multiple miRNAs, creating a complex regulatory network with significant impact on cellular homeostasis.

In the context of stroke, miRNAs have been shown to play critical roles in virtually all stages of the ischemic cascade:from excitotoxicity and oxidative stress to inflammation, apoptosis, angiogenesis, and neuroregeneration. For example, miR-21 is significantly upregulated following ischemic stroke and is known to promote neuroprotection by inhibiting apoptosis through the down-regulation of pro-apoptotic genes such as PDCD4 and FasL. Additionally, miR-21 enhances angiogenesis by targeting PTEN, thus activating the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, which promotes endothelial cell survival and proliferation. Another micro RNA, miR-126, highly expressed in endothelial cells, contributes to maintaining vascular integrity and regulating leukocyte adhesion by targeting genes like VCAM-1 and SPRED1. After a stroke, increased expression of miR-126 has been associated with improved BBB function and reduced vascular inflammation, positioning it as a potential therapeutic target for vascular repair. Furthermore, miR-210, often referred to as one of the most prominent "hypoxamiR (specific subset of miRNAs whose expression is regulated by hypoxia)," is induced under hypoxic conditions and promotes angiogenesis and cell survival during cerebral ischemia by regulating genes involved in mitochondrial metabolism and vascular remodeling. miR-124, one of the most abundant brain-specific miRNAs, is implicated in modulating neuroinflammation by targeting components of the NF-kappaB signaling pathway, while also playing a role in microglial polarization toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype. Several circulating miRNAs have also been proposed as potential diagnostic or prognostic biomarkers for ischemic stroke. For instance, elevated plasma levels of miR-122, miR-125a-5p, and miR-145 have been associated with stroke severity and infarct volume, although larger cohort studies are needed to validate their clinical utility. Collectively, these findings underscore the critical role of miRNAs in the molecular pathogenesis of stroke. Their spatiotemporal expression profiles, combined with functional specificity, make them attractive targets for therapeutic modulation. However, challenges such as off-target effects, delivery across the BBB, and temporal control of expression must be addressed before miRNA-based therapies can enter clinical practice.
Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs)

lncRNAs are RNA transcripts exceeding 200 nucleotides that, despite lacking protein-coding potential, serve as key regulators of gene expression at multiple levels, including chromatin remodeling, transcriptional regulation, and post-transcriptional processing. In the context of stroke, lncRNAs have emerged as important modulators of diverse pathophysiological mechanisms such as neuroinflammation, apoptosis, angiogenesis, and BBB integrity. Their regulatory actions occur through several distinct mechanisms. Firstly, in chromatin remodeling and transcriptional regulation, lncRNAs can recruit chromatin-modifying complexes to specific genomic loci, thereby altering the epigenetic landscape and modulating gene expression. Certain lncRNAs interact directly with histone-modifying enzymes to either activate or silence transcription. Secondly, at the post-transcriptional level, lncRNAs can bind messenger RNA (mRNA) transcripts, influencing their splicing, stability, and translation efficiency and thus modulating the synthesis of proteins relevant to stroke pathology. A third key mechanism involves their function as competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs); in this role, lncRNAs act as molecular sponges for miRNAs, sequestering them and preventing miRNA-mediated repression of their mRNA targets. This ceRNA activity adds a layer of post-transcriptional control over gene expression during ischemic injury.

Several lncRNAs have been functionally characterized in the context of stroke. MALAT1 (Metastasis Associated Lung Adenocarcinoma Transcript 1) is upregulated following cerebral ischemia and has been shown to promote angiogenesis and neuroprotection by modulating endothelial function and inflammatory signaling, thereby supporting vascular repair and neuronal survival. MEG3 (Maternally Expressed Gene 3) is another lncRNA implicated in stroke, primarily through its role in promoting neuronal apoptosis. It interacts with the p53 signaling pathway to activate pro-apoptotic genes, thereby exacerbating ischemic injury. H19, a well-known lncRNA involved in embryonic development, has been found to regulate inflammation and oxidative stress responses in the ischemic brain. Elevated H19 expression in stroke models contributes to neuronal damage via modulation of several stress-related signaling pathways.

Additionally, ANRIL (Antisense Non-Coding RNA in the INK4 Locus) has been linked to both atherosclerosis and stroke risk. It regulates gene networks related to cell proliferation and inflammation, thereby influencing vascular pathology associated with stroke. The functional specificity and dynamic regulation of lncRNAs in stroke pathophysiology also underscore their potential as therapeutic targets and diagnostic biomarkers. Therapeutically, manipulating the expression of lncRNAs:either by inhibiting deleterious ones, such as MEG3, or augmenting protective ones like MALAT1:could offer novel strategies for mitigating ischemic damage. Furthermore, lncRNAs circulating in the blood or CSF have been proposed as non-invasive biomarkers for stroke diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring. Their ability to interact with miRNAs further enhances their regulatory scope, as they modulate key molecular circuits through the ceRNA network, influencing gene expression patterns central to stroke onset and progression. Collectively, these insights underscore the critical and multifaceted roles of lncRNAs in stroke biology, supporting ongoing efforts to harness them for clinical applications.
Circular RNAs (circRNAs)

CirRNAs are a distinct subclass of non-coding RNAs characterized by covalently closed loop structures, which confer enhanced stability and resistance to exonuclease-mediated degradation. Emerging evidence suggests that circRNAs play pivotal roles in stroke pathophysiology by acting as competing endogenous RNAs or "miRNA sponges," thereby regulating the activity of stroke-associated miRNAs. This post-transcriptional regulation influences downstream mRNA targets involved in oxidative stress, apoptosis, inflammation, and angiogenesis. For example, circDLGAP4 has been shown to protect against ischemic stroke injury by sponging miR-143 and modulating endothelial function and BBB integrity. Additionally, brain-enriched circRNAs such as circHECTD1 and circTLK1 are dynamically expressed following cerebral ischemia and have been implicated in regulating astrocyte activation and neuronal apoptosis, respectively. Their tissue-specific expression, temporal regulation during ischemia-reperfusion injury, and detectability in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma make circRNAs promising candidates for diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic intervention. Ongoing research continues to unravel the mechanistic roles of circRNAs in neurovascular remodeling and stroke recovery.
Personalized medicine and clinical implications

Advances in stroke genetics are ushering in an era of personalized medicine, where prevention and treatment strategies are tailored to an individual's genetic profile to enhance efficacy and minimize adverse effects.
Genetic testing for stroke risk prediction

Monogenic Disorders: Genetic testing is crucial for diagnosing monogenic stroke disorders such as CADASIL and Fabry disease. CADASIL is caused by mutations in the NOTCH3 gene, leading to small vessel disease and recurrent strokes. Early identification through genetic testing enables timely interventions and family counseling. Fabry disease, resulting from mutations in the GLA gene, leads to the accumulation of globotriaosylceramide, causing vascular complications, including stroke. Enzyme replacement therapy can mitigate disease progression if initiated early.

passages.text: Polygenic Risk Scores: PRS aggregate the effects of multiple genetic variants to estimate an individual's risk of stroke. Integrating PRS with traditional risk factors, like hypertension and smoking, improves risk stratification. Studies have demonstrated that individuals in the highest PRS quartile have a significantly increased risk of stroke compared to those in the lowest quartile. PRS can also aid in identifying individuals at risk for specific stroke subtypes, such as cardioembolic or large artery atherosclerotic strokes
Pharmacogenomics in stroke treatment
Antiplatelet Therapy:

Genetic variations in CYP2C19 influence the metabolism of clopidogrel. Individuals with loss-of-function alleles exhibit reduced drug efficacy, leading to higher rates of recurrent strokes. Alternative antiplatelet agents, such as ticagrelor, may be more effective in these patients.
Anticoagulation Therapy:

Variants in VKORC1 and CYP2C9 genes affect warfarin sensitivity and metabolism, necessitating dose adjustments to minimize bleeding risks and ensure therapeutic efficacy. Genotype-guided dosing can lead to more stable anticoagulation and reduce the risk of adverse events.
Statin Therapy:

SLCO1B1 gene polymorphisms can predispose patients to statin-induced myopathy. Genotype-guided statin selection and dosing can mitigate this risk. For instance, patients with the SLCO1B1 c.521T > C variant may benefit from alternative statins or adjusted dosing to reduce the likelihood of muscle-related side effects.
Implementation Challenges:

Despite the potential benefits, integrating pharmacogenomic testing into clinical practice faces challenges, including cost, accessibility, and the need for clinician education. Ongoing research and policy development are crucial to overcoming these barriers and realizing the full potential of personalized medicine in stroke care.
Future Directions in stroke genetics research
Integrative multi-omics approaches

Integrative multi-omics approaches, which combine genomics with transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, are expected to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying stroke. By analyzing multiple layers of biological data, researchers can identify how genetic variants influence gene expression, protein function, and metabolic pathways, leading to stroke. For example, combining genomic data with transcriptomic analysis can reveal how stroke-associated variants affect gene expression in the brain. Similarly, proteomic and metabolomic analyses can uncover biomarkers that reflect the biochemical changes occurring in stroke patients, potentially leading to the development of new therapeutic targets.
Precision medicine and gene therapy

Precision medicine, which tailors healthcare based on an individual's unique genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors, holds great promise for stroke prevention and treatment. Advances in gene-editing technologies, such as CRISPR/Cas9, hold promise for correcting disease-causing mutations in monogenic stroke disorders, including CADASIL and Fabry disease. Preclinical studies are already exploring the use of CRISPR to edit mutations in the NOTCH3 gene, which could prevent stroke in individuals with CADASIL.

Gene therapy is another area of active research, intending to deliver therapeutic genes to correct the underlying genetic defects that cause stroke. Although gene therapy for stroke is still in its early stages, it holds significant potential for improving outcomes in individuals with genetic predispositions to stroke. Major practical constraints remain across discovery and translation. Polygenic risk scores (PRS) for stroke show modest individual-level predictive value and limited transferability across ancestries; multi-ancestry methods and prospective utility trials are needed. Human iPSC-based NVU/BBB models improve fidelity but still face incomplete maturation, lack perfusion and immune components, and line-to-line variability. CRISPR/Cas-based interventions face BBB delivery barriers, off-target edits, and potential immunogenicity; brain-targeted delivery remains a key hurdle. Clinically, robust dose-exposure-response data for epigenetic/ncRNA modulators in acute stroke are sparse, and interactions with antithrombotics/antihypertensives require early-phase evaluation.
Conclusion

The last two decades have seen remarkable progress in understanding the genetic basis of stroke. GWAS, whole-exome sequencing (WES), and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) have unveiled numerous common and rare genetic variants linked to stroke, particularly ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke. These genetic discoveries have deepened our understanding of stroke's heterogeneous nature, emphasizing the complex interplay between genes, environment, and traditional risk factors such as hypertension and diabetes. Common genetic variants like HDAC9, PITX2, and ZFHX3 have been consistently linked to various ischemic stroke subtypes. Rare monogenic causes of stroke, such as CADASIL (caused by NOTCH3 mutations) and Fabry disease (resulting from GLA mutations), offer insights into specific pathways leading to cerebrovascular disease. Advances in functional genomics, particularly the use of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing technology, are now enabling scientists to investigate the direct effects of these variants in patient-derived models. Epigenetic mechanisms, such as DNA methylation and non-coding RNAs, have added an additional layer of complexity, revealing how environmental factors influence stroke risk at the molecular level. This growing body of knowledge is paving the way for personalized medicine, where genetic testing and pharmacogenomics will tailor stroke prevention and treatment strategies. The next phase should prioritize prospective, multi-ancestry human biomarker studies (serial blood/CSF and imaging) to validate genotype and epigenetic-based signatures for risk, subtype assignment, and prognosis. Rigorous pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic programs for epigenetic modulators (HDAC/DNMT, ncRNA) must confirm BBB penetration, target engagement, and exposure-response, and characterize drug-drug interactions relevant to acute care. Finally, molecularly enriched, adaptive trials should embed these biomarkers, pre-specify decision thresholds, and monitor safety, including hemorrhagic transformation, so that genetics/epigenetics can translate into tangible prevention and recovery gains.

A graphical abstract of an integrated visual summary of the genetic and epigenetic frameworks contributing to stroke susceptibility. The top panel illustrates key components, including common variants identified by genome-wide association studies (GWAS) such as HDAC9, PITX2, ZFHX3, COL4A1/A2, and LPA; monogenic disorders (e.g., CADASIL, Fabry disease, and sickle cell disease) with their causative genes (NOTCH3, GLA, HBB); and epigenetic mechanisms including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNAs. These elements collectively influence stroke susceptibility. The bottom panel highlights personalized therapeutic strategies derived from these molecular insights, including genetic testing, pharmacogenomics, CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing, and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based modeling. This figure summarizes the interplay between genetic, epigenetic, and transcriptomic mechanisms, underscoring their implications for individualized stroke prevention and treatment.

Mechanistic Pathways Linking Genetic Variants to Stroke Subtypes. This schematic illustrates the functional consequences of key genetic loci associated with different stroke subtypes. HDAC9 promotes large artery stroke via NF-kappaB-mediated inflammatory pathways. PITX2 and ZFHX3 contribute to cardioembolic stroke through altered cardiac conduction and atrial remodeling, predisposing to atrial fibrillation. Mutations in COL4A1 and COL4A2 disrupt type IV collagen, leading to endothelial dysfunction, blood-brain barrier breakdown, and susceptibility to small vessel ischemic stroke and deep intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH).

Genetic Variants and Mechanistic Pathways Across Stroke Subtypes: Summary of GWAS-identified and candidate gene associations stratified by stroke subtype, along with corresponding pathophysiological mechanisms.

passages.text: Influenza Vaccines: Current Status, Adjuvant Strategies, and Efficacy

The influenza virus is one of the major global health concerns, causing significant morbidity and mortality in both humans and animals, with substantial impacts on public health. Vaccination remains the primary strategy for managing influenza virus infections; however, the virus undergoes frequent genetic changes through antigenic drift and shift. These mutations lead to new seasonal strains that evade pre-existing immunity. These mutations can potentially result in virulent strains that could trigger future pandemics. Therefore, developing a vaccine capable of providing robust protection despite these genetic changes is essential. Vaccine adjuvants are essential for boosting and directing the immune system's response, broadening the spectrum of protection, and reducing the amount of antigen required to achieve protection, which is particularly valuable in the face of rapidly evolving strains and during pandemics. Recent advances in adjuvant design and formulation strategies have demonstrated promising improvements in both the overall potency and durability of influenza vaccines, importantly, significant reductions in losses due to influenza infection. This review highlights the current status of different types of influenza virus vaccines, their benefits, and challenges. Further, the review focuses on the role of adjuvants, discussing their advantages, limitations, and methodological approaches, while also considering their potential contribution in developing a universal flu vaccine intended to provide extensive and lasting protection.
1. Introduction

Influenza virus is a highly contagious pathogen that infects multiple species, including humans, pigs, and birds. It is a negative-sense, segmented RNA virus classified under the family Orthomyxoviridae. The virus is divided into several types: A, B, C, and D based on their genetic makeup, antigenicity, and host spectrum. The genomes of Influenza A and B viruses consist of eight RNA segments, while Influenza C and D viruses have seven segments. Humans, birds, pigs, and horses are among the hosts susceptible to Influenza A virus infection. Whereas the primary host for the Influenza B virus is humans, though also identified in seals. Influenza C infects primarily humans and pigs and occasionally infects dogs. Influenza virus D was recently identified as a livestock virus primarily affecting cattle with sporadic cases in pigs and goats. Among all influenza viruses, the Influenza A virus is considered the most pathogenic to humans, due to its ability to infect multiple species, undergo rapid genetic changes, and adapt to new hosts. The segmented nature of influenza A genomes permits the mixing of RNA segments from different strains within the same host, creating new viral variants. Such sudden changes (antigenic shift) have resulted in emergent strains against which little population immunity exists, potentially sparking pandemics. In addition, continuous antigenic drift (accumulation of point mutations) causes influenza viruses to constantly evolve, making it challenging to forecast which strain will dominate each season. Further, influenza viruses from animal origin remain a major global health threat because they can mutate or reassort to gain efficient human-to-human transmission, potentially sparking a severe pandemic (zoonosis).

Influenza virus infection could cause severe life-threatening complications in children, the elderly, and adults with long-term health complications such as diabetes, asthma, chronic kidney disease, or heart disease. In addition to causing health complications, Influenza outbreaks also add significant financial burdens to society. It is estimated that annual influenza infections add $87.1 billion in cost to the US economy and $6 and $14 billion to the European economy. A recent study in 2023, based on approximately 20 million influenza-related claims collected over five years (2015-2019), estimated that annual costs of influenza-related hospitalizations in the United States were about $8.0 billion annually.

Vaccination remains a highly effective strategy to prevent influenza infection and to limit its transmission. Based on surveillance of potential circulating influenza viruses, viral strains for the vaccines are selected that are likely to induce a protective immune response against the circulating strains. Influenza vaccines designed based on the surveillance data are typically formulated as either quadrivalent vaccines, containing two influenza A strains and two influenza B strains, or trivalent vaccines, which include two A strains and one B strain. Although this strategy has been effective, influenza viruses have a high mutation rate, particularly due to antigenic drift and occasional antigenic shifts, which complicates accurate prediction of dominant strains. Consequently, seasonal vaccines sometimes fail to completely match the circulating strains, reducing their protective efficacy. For these reasons, despite widespread vaccine availability, influenza still causes significant illness and deaths worldwide, and it remains a serious health concern. Further, protection from modern influenza vaccines is predominantly strain-specific, leaving individuals vulnerable to viruses that have drifted or shifted.

To address this limitation, the advancement of next-generation influenza vaccines incorporating novel adjuvants can significantly boost both the magnitude and durability of the immune response. Adjuvants play a pivotal role in enhancing vaccine efficacy by activating innate immune pathways, antigen presentation, and promoting long-lasting adaptive immunity. Their significance becomes particularly evident in the context of influenza vaccines, where antigenic drift, strain variability, and reduced responsiveness in vulnerable populations such as the elderly often limit protective efficacy. Several adjuvants have been identified for their potential to elicit cross-protective immunity against multiple influenza strains.

The primary objective of this review article provides a foundational overview of the influenza virus and examine conventional influenza vaccines, detailing their mechanisms of action and inherent limitations, particularly their strain-specific protection. In addition, it highlights the critical role of vaccine adjuvants in enhancing the immunogenicity and overall efficacy of current influenza vaccines, as well as their capacity to elicit broad, cross-protective immune responses. Finally, the review explores emerging strategies and innovative approaches aimed at improving influenza vaccine performance and shaping the future landscape of influenza prevention.
2. Methods

This review employed a narrative approach, aiming to provide a comprehensive synthesis of current knowledge on the influenza virus, the types of influenza vaccines available, their modes of action, and seasonal influenza vaccines, including trivalent and quadrivalent formulations. The review also focused on vaccine epidemiology, health outcomes, and related policy changes. A narrative review was chosen to allow a broad discussion of scientific, regulatory, and public health perspectives, rather than conducting a quantitative meta-analysis.

Relevant literature was identified through searches of multiple databases and official sources, including Google Scholar, PubMed, U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), World Health Organization, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA). Literature research was conducted from June 2024 to August 2025, without restrictions on publication date, including sources that provided peer-reviewed scientific evidence or information from official governmental and organizational websites. This approach allowed for the integration of emerging trends in influenza vaccine development, while retaining historical discoveries and foundational data essential for a comprehensive review. There was no language restrictions applied; however, only sources accessible in English were included. Inclusion criteria comprised studies, official reports, and guidance documents addressing influenza vaccine composition, effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, epidemiology of circulating strains, and public health recommendations. Exclusion criteria included non-peer-reviewed opinion pieces, unpublished data, and studies unrelated to human influenza vaccine. Being a narrative review, this study has inherent limitations. It does not employ systematic quantitative synthesis or meta-analysis, which may introduce selection bias. The results and conclusions rely on the availability and quality of published information and official reports during the specified timeframe. Nevertheless, the use of multiple reputable databases and regulatory sources provides a comprehensive overview of recent developments in influenza vaccination.
3. Influenza Virus Pandemics, Seasonal Outbreaks, and Zoonosis

Influenza viruses have posed a persistent threat to global public health through both sporadic pandemics and recurring seasonal outbreaks. The pandemic H1N1 1918, the H2N2 pandemic 1957, the H3N2 pandemic 1968, and the H1N1pandemic 2009 are the four major influenza pandemics in recent human history caused by the influenza virus A. The 1918 influenza pandemic infected approximately one-third of the global population and caused an estimated 50 million deaths, whereas the H2N2 (1957) and H3N2 (1968) pandemics each resulted in about one million fatalities. The 2009 influenza pandemic resulted in an estimated 151,700 to 575,400 deaths. The 1957 H2N2 pandemic virus contained three gene segments derived from avian influenza A viruses, while the 1968 H3N2 pandemic virus carried two avian-origin gene segments. In contrast, the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus possessed a unique genomic composition, and it contained gene segments originating from avian, human, and swine influenza A viruses. In addition to these pandemics, scientists have observed seasonal patterns in influenza virus infections, correlated with distinct waves in the northern and southern hemispheres. In seasonal variations, the influenza A virus undergoes frequent mutations, especially in its HA (Hemagglutinin) and NA (Neuraminidase) surface proteins. Influenza A virus has 18 distinct hemagglutinin (HA) subtypes and 11 neuraminidase (NA) subtypes. The combination of different HA and NA subtypes in the virus leads to distinct patterns of infection and severity in humans, resulting in seasonal influenza infections affecting millions of people each year. Among the Influenza A virus subtypes, only H1, H2, H3, H5, and H7 have been shown to infect humans. Although sustained human-to-human transmission is rare, avian influenza A subtypes such as H5N1 and H7N9 have occasionally infected humans and are associated with high mortality rates. The high mutation rate emerging from frequent replication errors in influenza virus genes is attributed to the lack of proofreading activity in its RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Non-structural genes of influenza A and B viruses have been reported to have annual mutation rates of around 2.0 x 103 and 0.6 x 103 nucleotide substitutions/sites, respectively. Such changes help influenza viruses avoid host immune surveillance and cause seasonal infections. Every winter, multiple seasonal influenza virus strains circulate, causing influenza infection. According to estimates from the World Health Organization (WHO), seasonal influenza virus infections result in three to five million cases of serious illnesses, which lead to 290,000-650,00 deaths annually worldwide. Influenza has a significant negative impact on human health, particularly in those 65 years of age, and is responsible for 50-70% of flu-related hospitalizations and 70-85% of flu-related deaths, even though the COVID-19 pandemic has caused a decline in influenza activity in recent seasons (2020-2021 and 2021-2022).
